speakeroldname: Mr. Richard Grise (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask that all questions be allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it agreed?
[DOT] (mo)

I want to bring to your attention that, under Standing Order 64 of the House of Commons, it is compulsory, when a Member has asked a question that it be replied to within 45 days. There is no exception, no means by which the Government can evade that particular responsibility. You will know, Mr. Speaker, that that is sometimes not done. By and large the House is cooperative with the government Members. Whenever there is a delay of a few days, Members usually extend their cooperation to the Government. However, we reach a point when our patience does come to an end.
Question 289 in my name has been standing on the Order Paper since March 15, 1988. To refresh your memory, Mr. Speaker, it relates to the number of contracts, awards, and
funds that were given to one Jean Sirois of Quebec City by the Government. That question has been on the Order Paper since March 15. The 45 day deadline has gone from 45 to 90 days and now beyond.
The Member across may think that the rules of the House are irrelevant. Perhaps that is the opinion of the Government, and perhaps that is why the question remains unanswered. As the custodian of the rules of this House, Mr. Speaker, I want to ask you if there is any means by which the Government could be compelled to reply to a legitimate question, one which is within the rules, and has not been challenged in terms of its legality, yet remains unanswered.
I have met privately with the Minister and suggested that, even if the list were not completed, I would be willing to offer my support at least to the tabling of the part of the answer that was available from the Government. Yet no reply even comes from that suggestion. The fact that the Government refuses to respond to this question obviously leads one to believe that the answer could potentially be one that would cause certain embarassment to the Government, therefore, it is withholding the information. If that is the case it is not right.
If there is another reason, I am willing to listen to what the reason is, and why the rules of this House are being breached in a cavalier fashion the way that they are in relation to Standing Order 64 as it applies to question No. 289 standing on the Order Paper of the House of Commons since March 15, 1988.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to contribute to this exchange of comments and remind the House that not so long ago, several weeks or maybe a month, I asked the Chair to look into the whole issue of the forty-five day limit. As the Hon. Member pointed out, the Government is supposed to answer a question within forty-five days, when so requested. When the Government fails to reply within forty-five days, as happens occasionally, no penalty is applied. No corrective action is taken, and we have no way of raising the issue in the House for debate.
I asked the Chair to look into the matter. Perhaps it has had time to consider the question and could give us an answer today or at least take the matter under advisement and refer it to the appropriate committee and ask the committee to see whether it would be possible to include corrective measures in Standing Order 64(3) and (6). It may be an academic question, but as far as the Standing Orders are concerned, it is frustrating for Members who put important questions to the


Canada Child Care Act
Government when they do not receive a satisfactory reply within the prescribed forty-five-day period. The Government says it can do nothing. True, except that we depend on the good faith and the good will of the Government to provide the requested replies, and if the Government does not want to do that, there are a number of solutions we can suggest to the Chair for obtaining satisfaction when a question has been asked.
The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) is quite right to feel insulted and to think that perhaps his privileges have been breached. He asked a question. I don't know whether it was embarrassing to the Government, and it is not for me to judge, but all I know is that we have a provision in our Standing Orders that says that the Government is supposed to answer within forty-five days of the question being tabled. It usually does that. It would seem that the Government does not want to answer this particular question. If that is the case, the Government should say so. At least we would know where we are!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the comments made by the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) and by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). I believe that in this situation, there is no question of the Government's being reluctant to answer a question. Mr. Speaker, I am inclined to believe that the issue here is the complexity of the question and the information to be provided the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. In fact, since this Government was sworn in four years ago, the Government has always acted to provide the House and Hon. Members with the maximum amount of information, as quickly as possible, so that the House can get on with its business and Members can get the information they asked for.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding I would like to make it clear to the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and also to the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier that the Government does not intend to evade the Standing Orders, including Standing Order 64(6). The Government's intention is to give each question put by Hon. Members the attention it deserves, but again. Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that occasionally, a question is so complex that it takes more time to obtain the information.
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary who has just risen in his seat has said absolutely nothing, with due respect. He told us that sometimes questions are complicated; that may be so.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is the answers that are complicated.

The Minister of Health is probably correct when he says the Government would be in a rather complicated situation if it tried to answer the question at hand. However, Mr. Speaker, I am still looking for a commitment from
the Parliamentary secretary. Will he or will he not answer the question pursuant to the rules of this House?
To refresh the memory of Members and of the Speaker, however, I am sure the Speaker is quite familiar with the rules. Standing Order 64(3)(b) states:
A Member may request that the Ministry respond to a specific question
within forty-five days by so indicating when filing his or her question.
Question No. 289 is marked with a number 2 beside it at the bottom of the page, which indicates that an answer is requested within 45 days. As far as I am concerned it is not a matter of choice that the Government has to have one of its Members stand in the House and state that he wants the House to know that this may be complicated. That is not good enough.
In order that Members of the House and all Canadians know what in fact I have asked of the Government, I have asked how many taxpayers' dollars-what is the amount of loot-that was given to Jean Sirois, a friend of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). That is all I want to know.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), and the Parliamentary Secretary for raising this matter.
As the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier so ably put it, under the existing Standing Orders there is absolutely nothing the Chair can do concerning this problem.
However I believe this is an important question which ought to be deferred to the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure. Perhaps I might urge the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier to make the appropriate request to the Hon. Member for Timiskaming to have the matter considered or possibly to improve the Standing Orders for the next Parliament.
Shall all questions stand?
Agreed.

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, September 16, consideration of Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and the amendment of Ms. Mitchell:

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion No. 38
That Bill C-144 be amended by deleting Clause 11.

Mr. Speaker, it is I think unfortunate that the House has not taken as close a look as it should have at some of the serious problems with this day care plan of the Conservative Party. As was stressed by some of our members in the debate, the number of witnesses was very severely constrained. The possibility of hearing witnesses from a variety of different parts of the country was prevented by the committee itself. As a result, we have a Bill reported back to the House containing some serious difficulties.
With these amendments we are attempting to do two things. First, to try to solve some of those problems. Second, to try to put in front of Canadians an alternative approach to day care. We think this approach would not only be much more efficient, would not only meet the needs of Canadian women and children much more effectively, but would do so in a manner which embodies strong national directions and objectives for day care of which we can be proud.
This particular amendment is complicated in that it attempts to remove a consequential amendment to the Bill dealing with the Canada Assistance Plan. CAP, as Members are aware, is the mechanism by which the federal Government provides support to people who cannot afford to meet expenditures which most of us are able to pay for, expenditures not only with respect to child care but in a large number of other areas with respect to their welfare. This Bill is a shift from the past approach of directing all federal Government support to child care through CAP. Consequently, the Conservative Government has to amend CAP itself in order to reduce the circumstances under which such child care assistance is distributed.
I want to take just a couple of minutes if I can to back up this amendment in the much broader approach which the NDP wants to take with respect to child care. I do it on the basis of two important pieces of evidence. The first comes from my own constituency of Essex-Windsor and the large number of people who are in need of day care there. The many different homes I visited over the past four and five years take care of children under ad hoc arrangements which do not have the kind of creativity, careful planning and attention to facilities which have to be there in official day care facilities. It is not that love for the children is not there on the part of the people running these ad hoc arrangements. Very often it is a case of the cost being low and parents choosing this arrangement because that is all they can afford. They cannot afford the official day care authorized by the provinces. Yet the need exists and it is desperate. I can think of thousands of people in my own constituency who share this need, and I suspect that close to two million children across Canada will not receive the kind of day care they should receive as a result of the Government's Bill.
Canada Child Care Act
Finally, on a personal note, I would like to tell Hon. Members that both my children went to day care facilities, which were excellent, official, inspected facilities, at a time when these facilities were less expensive and access was easier. Even at that time, however, there were waiting lists. My children found that experience to be tremendously stimulating and beneficial for them as individuals. They found it to be tremendously valuable in terms of their ability to work through the school system effectively and well in the future.
We are not talking only about solving a problem which exists for working parents, though that is important. We are also talking about creating a situation for children which will be much better than the situations in which many of them find themselves at the present time.
In a previous debate, I called for a child-centered policy for Canada. We do not have such a policy. When I hear people talking about eliminating abortion as being the heart of dealing with the problems of children, I say to them that the real answer is a child-centered policy that puts a decent day care strategy into effect. That is not what we will get with this Bill. That is why we have moved this amendment, and I hope it carries.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Just so that we all understand the process, did I hear you say that every one of those motions will be debated together but voted on separately?

speechtext: The Hon. Member is correct, with the exception that an affirmative vote on Motion No. 19 obviates the need for a vote on Motion No. 20 and a negative vote on Motion No. 19 necessitates a vote on Motion No. 20.

Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members should be aware of the fact that eight of the motions we are dealing with refer to Clause 3, the broadcasting policy. One motion refers to Clause 5, which deals with the objects and powers of the commission, and Clause 10, which falls under the regulations and general powers of the commission. One motion deals with Clause 44, which refers to the objects and powers of the CBC.
These motions are important and fundamental, yet they are very difficult to deal with all in one shot. I will, however, try to suggest to the Minister that these clauses need to be very seriously reviewed by the Minister. I hope the motions will find favour with her.
1 do believe it was the intention of the Minister to see that this aspect of the broadcasting system would reflect the concerns I will try to outline in my argument. Clause 14 relates to Part C of the broadcast policy for Canada. In outlining the broadcasting policy, we have neglected to express our desire for Canadian content and Canadian expression in a very direct way so that there is no misunderstanding on the part of the CRTC. The Minister's response-

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am sorry that I was tied up elsewhere when debate on Bill C-136 began.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Did you issue the writ? That's the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: You would really like me to tell you what is going on.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: I would like to indicate, for the purposes of debate on this grouping of amendments, that I am prepared to accept Motion No. 14, Motion No. 15 and Motion No. 21.
I thank the Minister very much for that information. Is that the motion which will recognize children and youth?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: Yes.
I am very pleased with that amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: It is just that the motion of the Member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) comes ahead of yours.

That does not matter. The Member's motion is along the same vein as mine. I am sure that that was a mere oversight. I am quite pleased that the programming goals will be clearly defined.
My next concern relates to Motion No. 17. The Minister has been good enough to accept Motion No. 14, and Motion No. 17 is directly related to it. It indicates the mechanism of how
Broadcasting Act
to make the system work in order that broadcasting undertakings, which include the programming undertakings, distribution undertakings, and network undertakings, operate within the Canadian system. It defines how we can ensure that it is recognizably and predominantly Canadian. I recommend to the Minister a review of that particular amendment. Perhaps we can hear about that when we vote on that amendment.
I point out to the Minister that since the Aird report of 1929 until the present there has been a continuing concern about the relatively limited amount of Canadian programming available on our Canadian channels. I need not remind the Minister of that, she has spoken about it at great length. We have been trying to ensure that we will have increased Canadian programming on our sets. As she well knows, since the spread of cable over 70 per cent of the English language television programs available to Canadians are foreign, for the most part American, and only 2 per cent of all the drama programming in English is Canadian while 10 per cent is French. We want not only made-in-Canada programs but programs which are reflective of Canada. Clause 3(l)(e) has weakened the possibilities of that and I strongly recommend a change in that regard.
With reference to the next series of amendments, our committee recommended very strongly that the developers, conceivers, and makers of the program should be responsible for them. The Minister has essentially made the cable companies, the carriers, responsible for the content of the programs which come through their systems. I suggest that that is unfair. The responsibility for programs which are broadcast should stop with the licensee.
The Canadian Bar Association presented a brief after our hearings. They brought to the Minister's attention the following:
In the new Act, by contrast, the term "broadcast", used as a verb, would probably be seen by a court as referring back to the definition of the word "broadcasting" in Section 2. Thus, paragraph 3(1 )(f) of the new Act would also impose a responsibility on distribution undertakings for programs they retransmit by wire, since such a retransmission would constitute "broadcasting" for the purposes of the Act, even though it only be "other means of telecommunications" not by radio waves.
So cable is included unfairly since, as you and I know, its primary function is to be a carrier. That is inconsistent with the Caplan-Sauvageau report, our broadcasting report, and the concern which the CCTA expressed. I ask the Minister to review what I perceive to be a very serious problem in this particular area.
The next area with which I would like to deal is that of educational broadcasters. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), in the last few days, addressed the importance of the problem of illiteracy which faces this country. He talked about allocating $110 million over the next seven years. That is not very much money but at least it goes in the direction of the concerns which I have raised consistently in our standing committee, particularly in relation to the creative use of captioning for the serious illiteracy problem which we have in


Broadcasting Act
our country. I am sure the Minister would agree with me that it is a bondage on one-quarter of the Canadian population.
Some adult Canadians who are able to read and write cannot understand what they are reading. They do not comprehend it. Illiteracy has been called the secret shame of Canada. One-quarter of the Canadian population cannot read the instructions on a soup label or the instructions on how to fill out their income tax return.
A creative approach to addressing this problem through the Broadcasting Act would be to run open captioning along with programs in many areas. Adults who are too ashamed to admit that they cannot read could learn by referring the writing under the pictures to the words they hear. This would be a most effective way to be good educational broadcasters.
The key problem is that there is no reference in this Bill to educational broadcasting as such. Instead, a reference is made to educational programs. That is embedded in Clause 3(1 )(r) which reads, "including educational and community programs".
The goal of my amendment is to focus on the role of the community and programmers, which are the responsibility of the cable system, and to separate that out from the role of the educational broadcasters. It is fundamental that the Broadcasting Act make provisions to license, by the CRTC, educational broadcasting services which are established by provincial Governments and that such services be regarded as an integral part of the Canadian broadcasting system.
The Minister herself told us, in her response on June 23, 1988, that there is no agreement among provincial Governments and broadcasters regarding a more specific reference in the new Act and that the existing arrangements, which define what constitutes educational broadcasting through an Order in Council, remain workable. However, it is not clear enough. The CRTC needs direction. The existing language in the 1968 Bill is satisfactory, and I recommend that we go back to Section 3(1) of the old Bill.
There is one last area which I would like to bring to the attention of the Minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, and that relates to Motion No. 55 which is with regard to the standards of programs and the allocation of broadcasting time for the purpose of giving effect to the programming objectives set out in Clause 3(1 )(f) and (h). The amendment which I have proposed would remove subclauses (f) and (h) and make the application to all of the broadcasting policy in Clause 3(1). It would set the standards for the entire broadcasting system. I would like to point out to the Minister that Clause 10(l)(c) presently contains all of the sections found in the Bill under Clause 3(1). I suggest that we move it into Clause 3(1).
I gather that I cannot speak to Motion No. 74 which I consider to be a very important motion. I hope-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would Hon. Members agree to give two more minutes to the Hon. Member in order to complete her remarks?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I would like to point out to the Minister that with respect to Motion No. 74, and this might have been an oversight, the motion relates to the fact that we have given a specific mandate for programming purposes to the CBC, as found in Clause 44. However, it creates a problem because it leaves out aboriginals and the disabled. I believe that is a drafting error. I would ask the Minister if she would be good enough to check this motion. I have already asked my colleague from Edmonton to check the motion since it was of concern. I think that it is strictly a drafting error. I hope that the Minister will entertain an inclusion of all of the concerns found under Clause 3(1), but in particular paragraphs (j) and (k), which set out the mandate of the CBC. I believe that the Minister would have wanted aboriginals and the disabled to be covered.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be here in the House after having flown overnight from Vancouver with my friend across the aisle, fresh and ready to debate this Bill today.
I want to thank the Minister for accepting these two amendments which I think are important. Motion No. 14, an amendment in the name of the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), is the same as my Motion No. 16. It was put forward by the Canadian production community. Without entering into a big debate about the matter in committee, we called it the "Night Heat" debate, something which is reflected in the statement of Paul Siren of the Canadian Conference on the Arts to the legislative committee when he described rather well the notion of producing Canadian programs that are distinctively Canadian and which reflect our culture. I am not talking about an American cop show which is made in Canada, but a cop show that is Canadian and which reflects our distinctiveness and culture. Some people call this a subtle distinction. It is not that subtle. It is a very important distinction. We have tried to include it in the Bill through this expression of encouraging the development of Canadian expression. I think this is good because in the future I see Canadians producing a wide range of programs for international markets in the global village. I see that we want it to reflect Canadian distinctiveness and culture.
Motion No. 15, which has been accepted by the Minister, would include children, along with men and women, in the Bill. This is very important for obvious reasons. Children spend so much time watching television. Thus the broadcast industry and the television networks, or the television that we are describing here, has to take into consideration the impact on children. This was a suggestion put forward by the Children's Broadcasting Institute and the Canadian Broadcast League, among others. I am grateful that the Minister has accepted it.


Motion No. 18 is a motion which I moved. I will try to explain it this way. The clause of the Bill with which it deals states:
(e) each broadcasting undertaking shall make maximum use, and in no case less than predominant use, of Canadian creative and other resources in the creation and presentation of programming-
There was a great deal of effort to have the word "predominant" included in the Bill. However, the clause continues:
-unless the nature of the service provided by the undertaking, such as specialized content or format or use of languages other than French and English, renders that use impracticable, in which case the undertaking shall make the greatest practicable use of those resources;
I think that is a clause through which a truck could be driven. Therefore I proposed the amendment to eliminate all the words after the word "programming".
A good example of what is meant by this is set out in a letter that I received from the Canadian Broadcasting League over the signature of Rose Potvin. She wrote this:
Dear Mr. Waddell,
The Canadian Broadcasting League was delighted, when we appeared before you, to learn that the Minister had agreed to amend Bill C-136 to include the "predominantly Canadian" phrase in the policy section of the Bill.
We have now received a copy of the Minister's amendments. The phrase has been included in Clause 3 but attached to it are so many qualifiers that virtually any broadcaster can claim an exemption.
As we stated in our presentation to the Legislative Committee there is no reason to water down the policy section of Bill C-136 as the CRTC has the discretion to allow lower levels of Canadian content for certain licensees either by condition of license or by regulation.
If there is any difficulty over "predominant", the CRTC can cover it. Let us not put these extra words in the Bill which I say will emasculate the use of the word "predominant". We will not be able to succeed in doing what we set out to do.
The private sector, according to various reports, including a House of Commons committee have stated:
Every royal commission and task force has said the same thing, and each of them-like the parliamentary committee-has then expressed the pious hope that private broadcasters would finally deliver what they promised when they were licensed. Year after year, the broadcasters have declined to do so-
In other words, they have promised to do better in terms of predominant Canadian content, something they never seem to deliver on.
Motion No. 20 would strike out line 21 at page 4 and substitute the following:
"high standard and should provide a reasonable opportunity for the public to be exposed to the expression of differing views on matters of public concern;
The clause which we are dealing with here in the bill tries to deal with balance. It deals with having balanced programming. Here it is deemed as a goal of the whole system to offer the public the right to be exposed to differing points of view on matters of public concern. We think, and this is why the amendment is here, that that should be the obligation of each broadcasting undertaking instead of the system as a whole. If it is made to be subject to the system as a whole then some station which everybody watches, for example in British
Broadcasting Act
Columbia, takes a very biased point of view, then another station, which hardly anybody watches, gives some room for the other side. We have met the whole standard for the system but it is not really fair and not really what we are attempting to do in terms of expressing a balanced point of view.
I know that this is a tough area, given free speech and guarantees of free speech and freedom of the press. However, I have had experience in British Columbia with this in election campaigns and other areas. It can be seen that these are public airwaves and these people do not own them. There has to be balance in them. Each broadcaster should be obligated to have that balance. We are not Americans in spite of how much the Government wants to make us Americans.
I believe Motion No. 21 was accepted by the Minister. It again would improve the human rights provision, and I congratulate the Minister on that. Of course during her political career she has always been open to women's issues long before those of us who were converted to that issue understood why it was so important.
Let me continue since I only have 10 minutes to deal with all the amendments. I thought the Government would consider accepting Motion No. 23. Motion No. 23 would amend Clause 3 by adding:
that broadcasting services reflecting the aboriginal cultures of Canada shall be provided where numbers warrant and as resources become available for the purpose.
This motion reflects the views of a number of aboriginal organizations that appeared before the legislative committee. The Bill as it stands makes reference to the need for alternate broadcasting services in the French and English languages. However, we believe that very little has been done to recognize and respond to the communications difficulties of our aboriginal peoples.
As it stands, the Bill provides little reason to believe that this situation will change.
Clause 3(n) merely suggests that programming that reflects aboriginal culture should be provided within the Canadian broadcasting system as resources become available.
As the Canadian Broadcasting League noted in its appearance before the legislative committee: "This gives provision for broadcasting services for aboriginal communities no priority at all".
We believe that the approach represented in our amendment is much more positive. It says that broadcasting services reflecting the aboriginal cultures of Canada should be provided where numbers warrant. In doing so, it adopts the language found in the standing committee report which was supported by members of all Parties. It would assure that aboriginal people have access, whether it be the South or the North, to broadcasting services that they themselves have a chance to control. A number of other groups that appeared


Broadcasting Act
before the committee addressed this issue. Our amendment would make aboriginal broadcasting more identified in the Bill.
While the Government recognizes English and French, the Bill is still behind the times in terms of dealing with multicul-turalism and aboriginal people.
Some cultural groups have said that this Bill should go through before this Parliament ends because if there is another extreme right wing Tory Government they may not even get this type of legislation.
These groups should think of the alternative, a New Democratic Party Government, or a government centre of the left in which the NDP has the balance of power. That would result in legislation that would really meet the concerns of the Canadian multicultural community and which would not be so tied into and impeded by the free trade deal.
While we appreciate the Minister's co-operation with respect to amendments dealing with children, women and human rights, we understand that over-all the Minister is hemmed in by the cultural implications of the free trade deal and an unwillingness on the part of the Government to attack the North Americanization of Canadian culture.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me say to the Hon. Member who just spoke that indeed there are groups who have indicated their willingness now to support this legislation. One of those groups is the La Coalition pour la defense de service franqais de Radio-Canada. Included under the coalition is the New Democratic Party of Quebec. I wanted him to know that that group is on record as supporting this Bill.
I want to comment on some of the proposals that have been made. I have indicated those amendments that I am willing to accept. I believe they strengthen the Bill.
On the other hand, there are several amendments which I cannot accept. For instance, Motion No. 17 would remove the reference to maximum and return to the status quo of "predominant".
The use of the word "maximum" extends to other groupings that cannot be predominantly Canadian the requirement to provide the maximum amount of Canadian content. That would not happen ordinarily, and it ties in directly with Motion No. 18.
I believe the amendment proposed in Motion No. 18 would indeed weaken the Bill because, in those rare instances where it is not possible to provide predominantly Canadian content, if that usage were eliminated, it is quite possible that the licenses that are given to them could be eliminated as well. For instance, classical music stations that do not carry a predominant by Canadian content would not be able to apply for and get a licence under this restriction. Others, such as Tele-latino or Chinavision would not be able to get a licence in that case.
First Choice would not be able to get a licence because the movies that are shown are not predominantly Canadian.
We have insisted that those areas which can indeed be predominantly Canadian will be predominantly Canadian. But we also want to insist that where possible, on classical music stations for instance, the maximum use is made of those compositions that have been written by Canadians and so on.
I do not want to weaken the Bill in any way. I think these amendments would do that.
Motion No. 22 deals with educational broadcasting. We have provided in Clause 3 the inclusion of educational and community programs. Educational programs are there in that fashion because we understand the importance of including educational programs.
However, I want the House to understand that this is different from the 1968 Act because the clause at that time was included for a very different reason. It was meant to include the use of the CBC transmitters because there were no educational systems in place at that time. Since then educational broadcasting systems have come into play in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and Quebec. They are operating now. They operate as well under federal-provincial accords, signed by Governor in Council. That has been discussed with provincial Governments across the country and that, indeed, is, it is felt, the best approach to follow with regard to educational broadcasting and the fact that education as such is a provincial responsibility. This has worked very well, and I think it will continue to work well.
The one other item that I want to mention is that I will take a look at the points raised by the Member from Mount Royal with regard to Motion No. 74. It is in effect a certain redundancy, but I will look to see whether or not that can be incorporated.

Mr. Speaker, I want to comment briefly on the amendments under consideration. I will read it because I think it is important:
"(ii) encourage the development of Canadian expression, providing a wide range of programming that reflects Canadian attitudes, opinions, ideas, values and artistic creativity, displaying Canadian talent in entertainment programming, and offering information and analysis concerning Canada and other countries from a Canadian point of view,".
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me this is an excellent amendment and, as I just said a moment ago, I am very pleased that the Minister chose to accept it. I would stress "Canadian" ... I beg your pardon?

That would weaken it, the way that that is phrased.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The Minister seemed to think this would weaken the Bill. Well, I would not want to argue with her about the value of her opinion on this.
Still, Mr. Speaker, I know it is important to insist that the Government should take into account the will of Canadians to continue strengthening the whole question of programming, to enable them to express their cultural aspirations through this medium. I simply want to make a few comments on the impact of the amendments before us.
Having given the Minister credit for generously accepting amendments Nos. 14, 15 and 21,1 want to say that like many others in this field I am disappointed that the Minister's Bill still needs to be reinforced, a Bill which I think seeks a Canadian solution but falls far short of the ideal solution.
This morning, for example, I read a Toronto Star editorial headlined "Broadcasting Act still badly flawed" which says that the Minister must not rest on her laurels but should continue to work and strengthen the Bill. It gives credit to my colleague from Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), telling her, and I quote:

"Liberal critic, Sheila Finestone, and her NDP counterpart, deserves credit for constructively criticizing a Bill that would clear our airwaves for further Americanization".

Of course, Mr. Speaker, the situation is not the same in the case of someone who speaks French, for he or she does not feel as seriously threatened by Americanization as does the anglophone majority of Canada.
But still I would simply point to a pervading factor in French television programming both inside and outside Quebec, namely the considerable number of American programs dubbed with French dialogue.
I thought that by creating this TV-5 Network, the Government would have realized the great need for Francophones outside Quebec to receive superior programming prepared by a network and a consortium made up of four or five countries, namely, Quebec, Canada, France, Belgium and Switzerland. But for us, outside Quebec, Mr. Speaker, this is an expensive proposition. As a matter of fact, in Quebec, those who want to suscribe to the cable systems offering the TV-5 signal, beside the other four channels must pay around $11.50 a month to get the basic package including the TV-5 channel, while those
Broadcasting Act
living in Ottawa or elsewhere outside Quebec must pay about $19.
Here, in my own riding, Skyline charges about $19 for the basic package-

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: It is different now!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Not yet. I spoke a few moments ago with some people in my riding who told me that they still have to pay $19, and the Minister says that such is not the case, that it is going to change!

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: Patience, patience!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Patience! Goodness gracious, I have been patient for a great many years and people keep telling me that I should be patient and wait. But the fact is that on September 19, 1988, Francophones outside Quebec living in the Ottawa- Vanier riding must pay to Skyline over $19 a month to get the package which includes TV-5.
So, I see a major difference between the $19 which I must pay to get the TV-5 channel and the $11 which my friends have to pay in Quebec. I feel that is a major difference.
As to the Canadian content-
There is no Canadian content!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
There is indeed a Canadian content! This TV-5 channel which I feel is excellent for education and information purposes, is a scheme which was put together during the Sommet de la francophonie in Quebec City to meet the needs of all Francophones who want to be ... how should I say . . . nourished by a television which is sensitive to their concerns.
To me there is a flaw and something is lacking. Perhaps the Minister has an answer in mind to address my concern telling me that I have nothing to worry about and that I should not be so impatient. But the fact remains that on September 19, 1988, that is today, there are Francophones in Ontario as in New Brunswick who find it impossible to suscribe to a cable network offering the basic package they want, including the TV-5 channel.
One of my constituents to whom I was talking a while ago suggested that perhaps we should insist on cable networks offering a basic package with two French channels, that of Radio-Canada-that one is always there-and some other.
I must admit that I do not have the answer, because cable distribution networks are a monopoly granted by the CRTC to groups of people which are concerned above all with providing their customers with what they want. But I suggest there might be a solution which the Minister could thoroughly examine and which would make it possible for Francophones living outside Quebec to have access to the TV-5 channel. We


Broadcasting Act
should not overlook the fact that it is the Federal Government which has assumed the rather high cost of this whole new TV-5 experience. There has been a major Federal Government involvement to help the TV-5 channel succeed.
Since Canadian taxpayers contributed to the setting-up of this network, I suggest the Minister should at least ease my concern by telling me that I will get a reply shortly.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On debate the Hon. Member for Mount Royal.

Mr. Speaker, I can see that we are going to do extremely well today. I am delighted, and I thank the Minister for the reconsideration. We are looking at broadcasting policy as it affects the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I will address the recommendations accepted by the Minister in a moment. First, I would like to address my first motion, Motion No. 25.
The general thrust of Motion No. 25 is the consideration that we would require that programming provided by the CBC should include a significant contribution from the Canadian independent production sector. This would ensure that the CBC would use independent producers in a variety of areas, not only for drama, but also for information and enlightenment programs within the CBC.
I understand that the CBC does have in house personnel. It conducts the finest of training, and those people are then available as the pool grows for the private sector and, potentially under this Bill, for those who will be working to produce programs in the distribution sector. Notwithstanding that, we have included the independent production sector in the general body of the Bill. I believe it is in Clause 3(h). The Minister has included the word "enlightenment" to make the mandate of the CBC more specific and clear. I wonder if the Minister wants to give some consideration to including that which she has done for the private sector, the independent production sector.
I am delighted that the Minister has accepted Motion No. 27 proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). However, his riding will be changing soon. We will see what happens there.
I certainly support the amendment that has been brought forth. I am pleased that the Minister will support the multicultural nature of Canada. Needless to say, the Ethnocultural Council and the Canadian Race Relations Group will be quite delighted with this particular amendment.
Did the Minister state that she was accepting Motion No. 29?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: Yes.

That is the clarification of the word "element", and I believe that the Minister has accepted it. I believe that we should extend a word of thanks to the Canadian Bar Association for the clarity and depth of its evaluation of the whole system. It has been very helpful in enabling us to improve this Bill all along the way. I wish to give a deep word of thanks to the bar association, to the Minister, and her staff for recognizing that that recommendation was worthwhile.
I certainly support Motion No. 30. I brought forward an amendment. However, it was not received with favour. This is an excellent amendment. It brings back the concepts that were found in the original 1968 Bill and puts the educational
broadcasters front and centre, which is where they should be. They have a very important role in Canada. Children watch more television than they spend hours at school, there are adults who have learning problems, and there are various aspects of training and retraining in a global economy which is changing so rapidly. They can be enabled, helped, and guided through the educational broadcasting system. I am very pleased to support this motion of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Kingsway, which states:
"(m) educational broadcasters reflecting Canada's provinces are key elements in the Canadian broadcasting system;"
I believe that it is fundamental for Canada and the federal Government to take the leadership and ensure that we not only support, but promote educational broadcasters across the land, and ensure that they fit into what the Minister has described as the public and private elements which make up the Canadian broadcasting system. They are a part of the public element of the broadcasting system.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak to a couple of the motions, and my colleague from Hamilton Mountain will speak on the last one dealing with the educational aspect.
First I want to thank the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) for mentioning that I will indeed be running in another riding.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: Which one?
It is called Port Moody-Coquitlam. That is one of the reasons I can hardly stand today. I ran in the Terry Fox Run at Port Coquitlam.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: I did it twice.

The Minister ran twice. I ran just once and I have trouble standing up today, but it was sure worth it. I saw Mrs. Fox personally and that was really something.
I certainly support Motion No. 25, the amendment put forward by my friend from Mount Royal. It says the CBC should have a significant contribution from the independent Canadian production sector. That is an important amendment.
I thank the Minister for accepting our Motion No. 27, which is designed to make the system reflective of the multicultural nature of Canada. I learned something in committee that I would like to pass on in commenting on this part. Mr. Fo Niemi of the Centre for Research Action on Race Relations gave an excellent brief, mostly in French. He said that it is precisely because President Juneau himself and Executive Vice-President Bill Armstrong always confuse two things that the mandate to reflect multiculturalism at the CBC should be included in the Act. They always seem to confuse multiculturalism and internationalism. They mentioned the coverage by the media of the events in Haiti and the culture and development of China. What has this to do with multiculturalism, he


asked? Multicultural programming for Canadians within the Canadian context is to reflect the diversity right here at home.
So he said to our friend, Mr. Juneau, President of the CBC, who I called the George Bush of Canadian politics because he has been in so many roles but never been elected to any. Mr. Juneau had a rather heated reaction to that one.
I must admit that I would confuse it, too. The point is, do not confuse international programming with multicultural programming. It is not the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: Absolutely.

However, I want to say this to the Minister and she should remember it. We still feel strongly, in spite of these provisions being put in the Act, that there is something outside the Act that runs with it, that is, it is all very well to give the CBC an updated mandate as defined in this Act, but if you do not give it any money, if you cut back as the Conservative Government has-

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: Come on now, Ian. Don't say that with a straight face.

It is absolutely true. Some 28 per cent of regional programming has been cut back, to the tune of $29 million. The reason for that is that the CBC has to get more money to produce its drama and so on and it has done it centrally. It should have had more money from the Government rather than cut-backs. In 1984, in real dollars, the CBC budget was $905 million. In 1985 it was $826 million. In 1986 it was $806 million. In 1987 it was $789 million. In 1988 it was $775 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: That is a lot of nonsense.

The Minister recently gave $20 million to the English service and $50 million to the French service. However, it is a fact that the Conservative Government, especially in the early part of its term with all those back-benchers who hate the CBC, cut it back quite dramatically. The effect has been to downgrade regional programming, and those of us from Vancouver feel that strongly.
As well, and the Minister knows this very well because she presumably has to fight for it in Cabinet, you must have an increase in funding for the CBC in order to deal with the mandate, or, at least level funding. As a matter of fact, in a recent report, the Conservative Chairman of the Standing Committee said 250 million new dollars annually was needed. That is a far cry from what the CBC is getting.
Dale Goldhawk of ACTRA said while the CBC is expected to fill a wide mandate, the money to do so just is not there. "In short, this part of the announcement does not exactly make my socks roll up and down". Rather well put. He was referring to the Minister's recent announcement. I know the Minister does not like to hear this. She sits there a little frustrated by it.
Broadcasting Act

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: She has added all that money. Now say that.
The Minister has added money recently, but I dare her to dispute my figures on the CBC's budget over those particular years going from $905 million to $775 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: It is now $1.1 billion.

We are talking real dollars. We know it has been cut back. Ask anyone in the regions and they will tell you.
The final motion is Motion No. 30 which deals with educational broadcasting. I see my time is running out so I will let my colleague, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar), speak on that.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, want to congratulate the Minister on the amendments she has allowed this morning. They will make it a much stronger Act. However, I am very concerned about Motion No. 30. It should be allowed because not only does the Bill not allow for educational broadcasting as a priority, it downgrades the amendment made to the Act in 1968 in this respect. That is the part we are concerned about. The fact that we need an agreement with the provinces to treat educational broadcasting as a priority was in the Act in 1968 and now that it is not there, it is downgraded.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: No, it is not.

My understanding is that the 1968 Act says that facilities should be provided within the Canadian broadcasting system for educational broadcasting. We want this to be strengthened so that educational broadcasters reflecting Canada's provinces are key elements in the Canadian broadcasting system. That is not being allowed to stand.
Bernard Ostry has looked at this very conscientiously and critically in response to the federal Government's refusal to respond sympathetically to repeated constructive suggestions from educational broadcasters from across this country, and its inaction on issues central to the future of educational television. He said the effect of the proposed legislation on educational broadcasters and the people we serve cannot be underestimated. This is not just some other piece of legislation. The Broadcast Act is to one of the largest industries in Canada whose product touches the lives of every man, woman and child in this country what the Criminal Code is to the administration of justice.
I think one of the things we are particularly concerned about is the great strength of the Broadcasting Act and how it can serve the people of this country, and the ability of the educational networks to be able to reach out to the people. Certainly of great concern to us these days are the people who are illiterate. We have seen some of the programs put forward by the educational networks and their ability to reach people that otherwise would not be reached.


Broadcasting Act
I think as well we would be giving our aboriginal people some priority in the Act. I have had great concerns about the fact that even though our amendment was not so strong on the aboriginal people and we were allowing it to say "where numbers warrant" the Minister has not accepted that amendment either. When we get into great debates about the illiteracy of our country and the inhuman way we have treated our aboriginal people over the years-I am certainly not saying that in any partisan context but in the context of how we have evolved as a society-that there could be within this Bill the ability to strengthen the educational networks and at the same time share with the rest of Canada the great riches of our aboriginal people through broadcasting. In my view, this is a very valid amendment that could strengthen the Bill. I hope the Minister will look at it again and allow it to stand so that we could have that kind of strength in this Bill that is so important for the educational networks.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in support of the two motions now before us, since Motions Nos. 27 and 29 were accepted by the Minister, something I thank her for. I would like to refer in particular to Motion No. 30 that deals with a matter of great importance to me. If I may read the amendment again:
(n) Educational broadcasters reflecting Canada's provinces are key elements
in the Canadian Broadcasting System;".
To me this statement seems quite realistic and accurate. Educational broadcasters did not exist in 1968, at any rate when the Act was passed, at least not in Ontario; TV Ontario did not exist in 1968. Having worked, as I said in this House, for nearly eleven years and some months in education in Ontario and having been instrumental in launching the idea of an educational TV system in Ontario, I find it unfortunate that the Minister cannot respond positively to our proposal not to decrease the importance of educational television, but at least leave the matter as it was in the 1968 Act.

The 1968 Broadcasting Act at Clause 3(i) stated:
-facilities should be provided within the Canadian broadcasting system for
educational broadcasting
This is what we call a stand-alone clause for broadcasters who wanted to go into educational television. Even though the Minister may disagree completely with those of us who think that she is downgrading the educational broadcaster by removing that stand-alone clause and putting in a clause which in our view groups the educational television with community programs, any broadcaster could say that he is meeting the requirements of the Bill because his programming is in keeping with it and does include educational and community broadcasting.
I know the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) just quoted from a release put out by the Chairman of
TV Ontario. Mr. Ostry in his plea to the Minister asked that she change the wording of the Bill to allow for this kind of stand-alone clause, but let me quote Mr. Ostry. He expressed:
-our profound disappointment in both the current hasty, eleventh hour process and its outcome.
Now is hardly the time to downgrade the standards of educational television originating in the regions. Indeed, it is a paradox that, at a time when the federal Government is, quite properly, committing millions of dollars to battle the problem of adult illiteracy in Canada, when the Prime Minister is endeavouring to encourage the development of a new "science culture", and when educational issues about skills training and multiculturalism command headlines in our news media, this proposed legislation appears to go out of its way to shove educational broadcasters out of "the system"
This comes back to the argument, and the Minister knows it, of how you define education. Maybe we could argue that there is a role for private broadcasters, a constitutional role that they may be able to displace or take over educational domains that are of provincial jurisdiction. I feel strongly that the Chairman of TV Ontario in my province, who is a well-known, serious and reasonable man, would come out so strongly condemning the present legislation and saying it is too weak. I hope the Minister will see the light as she did with the other two amendments in this grouping and accept, reply or assure us that she has absolutely no intention of muddying the waters between the provincial authorities on educational TV, the broadcasters or those who are lucky enough to have licenses given to them. I would not want us to see a few years hence have educational TV downgraded to the extent that it cannot operate or compete or see that its mandate has been weakened.
Before I end my remarks on this question, Mr. Speaker,
[ Translation]
. .. Mr. Speaker, let me make a simple clarification. Earlier I referred to TV-5, and I would like to clarify matters. I stated inaccurately that in Quebec the charge was $11 and some pennies, while in fact it is exactly $14.32. I checked earlier. I must admit this is a matter of great concern to me, and I simply wanted to come up with accurate figures to avoid being told: Jean-Robert, you were off the mark, the charge is $14.32. Therefore, for the record, Mr. Speaker, the charge in Quebec is $14.32 for basic service, including programs from the four channels: The Canal Famille, the Meteo-media, Musique Plus and YTV in English, plus of course TV-5, while in Ontario we have no access to that basic programming and we must pay $4 a month in decoder rental plus $2 in service fees, so that in French-speaking Ontario areas, we have to pay some $6 more than in Quebec to get the service that, as I emphasize, is less extensive than that available in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to add my support to the amendments which we are discussing and to urge the Minister to accept them.


I note, and put on the record as I think others have done, the views of the President of Knowledge Network, Mr. Glenn Farrell, who said in respect of this Bill:
The amendments to Bill C-136, proposed by federal Communications Minister Flora MacDonald are inadequate because they fail to recognize the important role that educational broadcasters play in Canada. This Bill downgrades the role of educational broadcasters at a time when regional communications are increasingly important.
There is not a Member of Parliament who has young children or young grandchildren, as 1 do, who cannot help but realize how much more knowledge our young people between the ages of four and eight or four and ten have about matters than children had 10 or 20 years ago. This is so because they have the opportunity to watch educational programs like Sesame Street and many others too numerous for me to report on. Any Bill which does not expand the ability of TV to disseminate more and more educational programming is deficient.
I want to speak about another aspect of the Bill, dealing not just with children. For almost as many years as I have been a Member of Parliament, I have raised questions about the fact that 20 per cent of the people of Canada are functionally illiterate, this at a time when we know that businesses, industries and farmers are facing increasing competition, making it tougher and tougher to be a success. Other countries have moved ahead of us because of their knowledge and ability to use the newest technology. How could the 20 per cent of Canadians who are functionally illiterate possibly find jobs, even if we lived in a period of full employment in that future when they do not have the ability to fill the jobs which are or will be available.
In the 1984 Throne Speech of the Government was a promise that dealing with illiteracy was to be a major objective of this Conservative Government. Silnce then virtually nothing was done by the federal Government, much too little is being done by the provincial Governments, and the voluntary organizations working in the field do not have the financial ability to do the job they want and need to do.
Four years have gone by and suddenly, two weeks ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) resurrected this important question, which he ignored for four years, and announced that the Government is proposing to spend over $100 million in the next four years dealing with illiteracy. We know that 20 per cent of the people of Canada are functionally illiterate, but nobody has any real information on the numbers of people who are attending programs organized by the provincial Governments and by volunteer organizations such as Frontier College or one such as that just started less than a year ago with offices in the constituency of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper), called Beat the Street.
Nobody knows how many people are in the programs. As a matter of fact one of the little tasks I have set for my staff is to get in touch with every such organization across Canada to
Broadcasting Act
find out how many people are in these programs. I have some idea of the information they will get. We will find that probably fewer than 5 per cent of the five million people who are functionally illiterate are in programs that will help them.
My colleague, the Hon. Member from Hamilton, has talked about the problems of native people. In cities like Winnipeg, Regina or Vancouver, to mention just three, one cannot help, if one drives around these cities, but note the tremendous movement into the cities of native people from the reserves. They come to the cities and their ability to speak English is far from what it should be. Many of them are in fact functionally illiterate.
In these cities, there is a time bomb which is ticking away and which will explode. Dealing with illiteracy is just one of the questions that we have to address if that time bomb is in fact not to explode. One of the ways it can be dealt with is by giving the broadcasting system, radio and television stations, public and private, not only the right to put on educational programs but the resources to do the job. Perhaps, for the private sector, we need legislation which will force the broadcasters to do some of the educational and cultural things they promised to do when they got their licences and which in fact they almost completely ignored once they were successful in getting the licenses. What they have concentrated on is having the right, as I think the Caplan-Sauvageau Commission has pointed out, to virtually to print money and make tremendous profits in return on their investment.
This is the situation we are in. It is a very desperate situation, it is a very serious situation. It is a situation which needs to be dealt with in every possible way. One of the ways is to amend this Bill so that the Broadcasting Act will make it very clear that radio and television stations and the networks have the right, and I would say the responsibility, to increase and improve educational programming. We need this amendment in the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, the fourth estate in Quebec is in mourning after the death of Jacques Beauchamp. It is somewhat of an institution that has disappeared, Mr. Speaker.
The very prolific sports writer and public relations vicepresident of the Journal de Montreal died of a heart attack at the age of 61.
Jacques Beauchamp made a name for himself in Quebec and throughout the rest of Canada. He loved his job and was a tireless and honest worker. Sporting events were his forte, and the men and women who got to know him will tell you that he was a hard and valiant worker respectful of others, a demanding but generous and inspiring man. subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO HYDRO QUEBEC POWER LINE ROUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Algonquins of Barriere Lake are currently blockading the construction of a Hydro Quebec power line from the townsite of La Domaine to Rapid Lake, their present reserve. The Algonquins of Barriere Lake oppose the construction of the line through La Verendrye Wildlife Reserve for good reason. A sum of $3.8 million is to be spent by the Department of Indian Affairs on a power line opposed by the very people for whom it is supposedly being built.
Why, you ask? Because the traditional uses and occupancy of the land by the Algonquins are already being severely eroded by hydro developments, road construction, industrial activity, hunting, and so on.
The Algonquins ask, what of the recognition and affirmation of their rights in Section 35 of Canada's Constitution? Must there be a confrontation, must all developments be halted, before the federal and provincial Governments sit down and listen?
I have tried, as have the Algonquins of Barriere Lake, to get the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and Premier Bourassa to listen. The Algonquins call for a fair settlement, for conservation, and for a sustainable approach to their homeland. Canada and Quebec must listen and learn.
These lands were set aside as Indian territory by the Royal Proclamation of 1763. Canada and Quebec must respect the rights, title, and agreements with the First Nations.

subtopic: PRESENCE OF TOXIC CHEMICALS IN FOODS
PRESENCE OF TOXIC CHEMICALS IN FOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the Ontario Government released a study showing that a wide variety of foods purchased in the province contain low levels of dioxins, dibenzofurans, and other toxic chemicals. This study confirms the results that Dr. Kate Davies of the Toronto Department of Public Health found in 1986.
Dioxins and furans are two highly toxic families of chemicals that come from the production of pesticides and wood preservatives and pollute the air when garbage is not burned at high enough temperatures. One kind of dioxin, TCDD, is believed to cause cancer in people. Scientists speculate that dioxins, furans, and PCBs create a reaction in the human body that may lead to increased cancer, inhibition of the immune system, and changes in hormones which, among other things, control the ability to reproduce.
The question we must ask ourselves is whether any level of these chemicals in food is a safe level. It seems to me that most Canadians would answer that the only safe level is zero.

The Niagara River was the largest toxic garbage pail ever imagined, but last year, for the very first time, a Niagara River Clean-up Agreement was signed.
We have passed an Environmental Protection Act with teeth in it.
The Canadian Water Conservation Act allows us to control our own water.
Canadians are demanding action for a clean Canada. This Government has listened, has acted, is acting, and will deliver on this as it has on other things.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bonita Clark's long ordeal has ended. I rise today to pay tribute to her courage and perseverance in battling an issue of major importance to women in the workforce. Canadian women owe a debt of gratitude for her seven-year struggle to have sexual harassment on the job recognized as a health and safety hazard.
Ms. Clark began to work as a stationary engineer at the Stelco plant in Hamilton in 1979. From her very first days on the job she was confronted with sexual harassment and gender discrimination. She recently succeeded in securing women their own washroom facilities at the plant, a basic necessity of decent working conditions.
According to the Human Rights Commission, sexual harassment is a reality faced by over 80 per cent of Canadian working women. Bonita Clark, by refusing to accept this reality and by protesting the health hazard posed by sexual harassment, provides inspiration to the women and men who are continuing her struggle to guarantee Canadians a workplace free of sexual harassment.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. In light of his recent commitment to the environment two weeks ago and the repeated requests of the Canadian Federation of Municipalities for the federal Government's share of sewage treatment and sewer separation costs, will the Government undertake today to assist municipalities with this program and help them to modernize and upgrade their projects at this time?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a puzzling question coming from such a source because the hon. gentleman was a Liberal Member of Parliament when the Liberal Government of the day in the late 1970s, 1980 and 1981 cancelled the broadly based federal government program which supported the provinces and, through the provinces, the municipalities for this very purpose. In the absence of the program when we took office in September, 1984, we resorted to, I think, very creative devices to assist cities where the national interest was advanced. For example, in the case of Montreal, there was the clean-up of industrial wastes in the St. Lawrence River. In the case of Halifax, there was the clean-up of the Halifax Harbour. That is the sort of creative, innovative mechanism of federal-provincial cooperation that has served Canada and especially the country's environment.

speakerposition: subtopic
Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question that begs to be asked is why be so selective? What about the national capital region? What about the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton which has repeatedly asked for assistance in modernizing and upgrading the installations in this community? Today the regional municipality wants to


Oral Questions
make the quality of life in Ottawa better by dealing with how we dispose of waste water.
I say to the Minister, never mind what happened then. I was there in 1976. Yes, we needed a program then, but what about a program today, 1988, to help the municipalities deal with that very expensive program? Flow about your power to spend? Use it.
Oh, oh!
That's the Liberal approach, spend, spend, spend.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Everybody else is getting it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can understand why the Hon. Member would want the country to ignore what the Liberal Party has done and said in the past in favour of what it is saying now. In any event, I mentioned the St. Lawrence River clean-up and the Halifax Harbour clean-up only as examples of the kind of major environmental undertakings the Government has launched. I could have mentioned, for example, the clean-up of the Hamilton Harbour through a federal-provincial mechanism that involved federal money being matched by provincial money for a very important anti-pollution control purpose. The national interest was served in that case and provincial jurisdiction was respected. Through federal-provincial harmony, "we did good", and I think we will do better.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and relates to patronage in the Pointe-a-Cascy development in the Vieux Port of Quebec, a project on federal land which gave rise to strong opposition from the residents of Quebec.
Can the Prime Minister explain why the Government has asked the firm of Eastern Quebec Conservative organizer Marc Lefranqois to develop this site, in spite of the evidence of his latest project, the Terrasses du Vieux-Port, where he will allow the disintegration of a site which has been designated as world heritage by UNESCO?
Is the Government prepared to take into account the historic and heritage quality of this site by drafting a development plan in close consultation with local residents, or does the Government think it is more important to make a gift to a Conservative organizer and friend of the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Science and Technology. The Minister set up a good program to allow Canadian students to compete for full four-year scholarships in the fields of science and engineering. However, I have been informed by a constituent of mine that the schools did not inform qualified students of this and that universities were given a set number of scholarships. As a consequence, students with high marks may not qualify while students with lower marks may get in.


Will the Minister investigate this and rectify the unfair occurrences?

speakeroldname: Hon. Frank Oberle (Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Science and Technology)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his interest in this matter. This gives me an opportunity, and I know all hon. colleagues would want to join me, to congratulate the first 2,500 of the 10,000 Canada Scholars who have received their first scholarships this year.
I would be disappointed if the message had not been properly communicated. On March 28 all of the schools were informed and 4,000 packages were delivered. The Prime Minister subsequently wrote a letter to every school pointing out, first, the need for the program and second, our intentions for it. Other efforts were made to get the message across as well.
Indeed, I can say that I am particularly proud that 53 per cent of the new scholars in the natural sciences and engineering programs are women, and we had excellent co-operation from the Canadian Association of Universities and Colleges. Of course, next year it is intended that the program will be subject to a national exam, and that would, I hope, eliminate any of the problems that may have been associated with the initial start-up of the program.
