Madam Speaker, it is going to be very difficult to debate all these issues in such a short time. However, we will give it a good try.
Motion No. 32 is a recognition of aboriginal languages. In the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture we recommended, in our sixth report, that a new Broadcasting Act should make provision for service within the Canadian broadcasting system in aboriginal languages considered to be representative, where numbers warrant, and to the extent that public funds would permit. The Government has not included this particular aspect in its subclause 3(m) of the broadcast policy. I would suggest that this is vital to the National Aboriginal Communication Society which brought this to our attention once again and expressed its dismay at the Government's failure to act.
I can recall sitting on the Indian affairs committee and working very hard on the amendments and the concerns of the aboriginal peoples of Canada. I really care about this aspect of the Bill. I know that my colleague presented a somewhat similar concern earlier in the day and I hope that, in a reasoned way, the Minister will see fit to give consideration to this motion.
Motion No. 33 is a very serious matter and I would like to suggest to the Minister, through you, Madam Speaker, that this motion does not oppose the service of alternative broadcasting in any sense. I am convinced, as are many people who came before our committee, that it is defined much too broadly within the Act and that we really do not need this to allow us to move ahead in any kind of a new broadcasting venture. We have moved into specialty services and pay-TV, and we have not provided place in the Act to undertake these kinds of activities. I do not think it is necessary and it causes confusion to the CBC mandate.
I suggest that this amendment removes all references to alternative programming in legislation. It is not needed, in my view. The way the alternative services programming mandate is defined is so nearly identical to that of the CBC and its role in the Canadian broadcasting system that I think this only serves to undermine the CBC and marginalize high culture and multicultural concerns which should be contained within mainstream productions as well as within the confines of the CBC.
ACTRA brought its serious concerns to our attention when it said in its brief that the alternative program system would
risk becoming a ghetto of programming appealing to very few people. In addition, because of this alternative programming services mandate in the Act, the other components of the system would be forgiven a requirement to participate in the production of minority or special interest programming and that would become the responsibility of the alternative programming service.
The standing committee, in its fifteenth report, in recommendation 100, recommended that the alternative television programming service to be created would be on a not for profit basis. This is not the approach the Minister has taken on page 35 in Canadian Voices Canadian Choices where she talks about a consortium approach for this service.
I would like to suggest to you that if, through consultation with the CRTC and interested parties, we do end up with the kind of Channel 4 format which you see in England, we might well be open and willing to having this kind of a program, but having this in the Act does not prevent that kind of thing. I suggest that this is premature. In fact, it is almost unnecessary. In the response that the Minister gave us the Government says that it is prepared to contribute substantially in these initiatives through new funding. I would like to recommend strongly to the Minister that if there is extra funding it should go to the CBC which has suffered some serious set-backs in its funding over the long term since 1984.
Motion No. 35 is divided into two parts. My amendment addresses both subclauses 3(q)(i) and 3(q)(ii). I believe the broadcasting law in Canada recognizes that the goal was to make programs that were made in Canada but also reflective of Canada. With regard to Clause 3(q)(i), my motion would require that broadcasting undertakings, that is network and programming undertakings, well, would require that programming be predominantly Canadian, as well as that there be predominant use of Canadian creative and other resources.
I know the Minister answered earlier, in response to subclause 3(l)(e), I believe it was, that it was so. I would like to remind her that if she looks at the amendment which I have proposed to that clause she will see that it keeps all the exceptions in place. It keeps the exceptions that we have all been very sensitive to such as Tele-latino and Chinavision, to use the Minister's own examples.
If you read Motion No. 35 you will see that I have indicated that private networks and program undertakings "shall provide programming that is predominantly Canadian, using predominantly Canadian creative and other resources in the creation and presentation of programming, unless the nature of the service provided by the undertaking, such as specialized content or format or use of languages other than English or French, renders that use impracticable, in which case the undertaking shall make the greatest practicable use of those resources".
I think that that would answer the concerns to which the Minister alluded earlier this morning, and I sincerely hope that for the sake of consistency and for the sake of the goals of the


Broadcasting Act the Minister will take serious interest in this particular amendment.
In subclause 3 (q)(ii) we refer to the private networks and the programming undertakings being responsive to the evolving demands of the public. I would like to point out to the Minister that not only have I shown some serious concern in this regard, but the CRTC brings the following observations. It says that the phrase "responsive to the evolving demands of the public" seems at first sight harmless enough. However, the specific object could have the effect of rendering the other general objects of Section 3 nullities. Would this specific object override the objects of high standards of programming, balance in programming, and programming for aboriginal peoples, for the disabled, et cetera? This section could cause needless litigation and may contradict an underlying principle of the regulation of the broadcasting industry, that is, that programming be of high standard and of quality.
I concur with the CRTC's view that we should amend this section. I suggest that private networks and programming undertakings should have the same responsibilities as those that are defined in subclause 3(l)(e) and that the Minister should put this clause in the Act to distinguish the role of the distribution undertakings, that particularly of private networks and specialty services or programming services, so that they have the obligation of Canadian programming along with the exceptions which I have just noted.
My amendment, in essence, is to bring consistency to the Act and to the possibility of the role of these undertakings. I suggest that the major objective is predominantly Canadian programming.
The next amendment, Motion No. 37, is a major area of concern with which I have had some ongoing problems. I would like to recommend to the Minister that the carriage regulations for cable are at least as important as the requirements for Canadian content quotas for broadcasting networks in maintaining any reasonable balance between Canadian and foreign programming in the system. I think that we must define cable and cable's role more clearly.
That is the ultimate goal of my Motion No. 37.
The standing committee felt very strongly about this aspect and there certainly has been no change in my view with respect to this particular motion. Motion No. 37 deals with the priority of carriage, with the complementary role that foreign services should play, and the exclusivity of the rights of those Canadian broadcasters who purchase programs and how they should be allowed to use them in the interest of the Canadian system.
The purpose of the Minister's focus, as I understand it, has been to bring the broadcasting system into a perspective that would develop the conditions whereby cultural sovereignty could be achieved. That was the goal of Mr. Bennett. It has
Broadcasting Act
been the goal of everyone who has been addressing this particular issue. I believe that goal is missing in this Bill.
I suggest that this motion is fundamental to the well-being of the broadcasting system and will ensure whether or not we have a Canadian broadcasting system or a North American system.

Madam
Speaker, we are dealing with a number of amendments. I wonder if the Minister accepts any of these amendments, but she is indicating that she is not.
This is a key part of the Bill in terms of the North Americanization of Canadian television. I did not expect the Minister to accept this amendment because in doing so she would have to go against the whole thrust of the Government's free trade initiative and the North Americanization that that embodies. I will say more about that in my speech at third reading.
This is a key part of the Bill because television is the most important cultural medium we have. Canadians, especially English Canadians, do not realize how our culture is potentially threatened by completely opening television airwaves to American programming.
Something can be done about this without hurting the choice of Canadians in watching television. That is the purpose of these amendments. These amendments respond to important recommendations of the sixth report of the standing committee. Motion No. 36 reflects recommendation No. 17 of the sixth report of the standing committee. Motion No. 39 reflects quite precisely recommendation No. 58 of the sixth report of the standing committee, a recommendation that was reiterated by recommendation No. 69 of the fifteenth report of the standing committee, which is the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture that has a Conservative majority. In recommendation No. 58 that committee stated:
The act should be drafted so as to define the essential role of distribution undertakings as that of distributing Canadian radio and television services in French and in English, both public and private, with first priority given to public-sector Canadian services, followed by private Canadian services. With the exception of the "three-plus-one" services already carried-
That is the American networks ABC, NBC, and CBS plus the American Public Broadcasting System. It continued:
-the act should make provision for the carriage of foreign radio and television services only when the programming they provide is complementary to that available from licensed Canadian broadcasters and network operators.
"Complementary" means that they are showing different programs or adding something that we do not already have. If we have a Canadian news network, we do not bring in the American news network. If we have a Canadian arts and culture network, we do not bring in American ones.
We have to be able to say no to bringing in the superstation from the United States. That is absolutely fundamental because without this provision American channels like the ones we are getting now, such as Ted Turner's CNN news, will


Broadcasting Act
come in. There are no similar Canadian programs. Once they are available, we must have the Canadian service.
The Conservative philosophy is simply to let them compete with Canadian programming. However, the Canadian market is too small and Canadians cannot compete. That is why the market theory falls apart. That is why, without these amendments, we could see the elimination of private broadcasters. That is why Global, CTV, and other broadcasters oppose this Bill. The Bill fails to implement those recommendations in the reports of the standing committee.
Motion No. 36 would ensure that all services operating in Canada, including U.S. satellite to cable services, are licensed. As the House knows, for example, the U.S. Arts and Entertainment Network is beamed into Canada by satellite and affiliates with cable companies that package and sell it to Canadian subscribers. It makes no contribution to Canadian programming and does not need to meet the requirements of the CRTC. In fact, it basically does not cost Arts and Entertainment anything to tap the Canadian market.
As the Association of Canadian Film and Television Producers said before our standing committee:
It would be consistent with the government's stated policies for broadcasting in Canada to require all broadcast services available in Canada to be subject to CRTC regulation and approval. The CRTC has a demonstrated sensibility to the needs of broadcasters and the government's policy priorities. We should all be confident in the Commission's ability to develop a realistic licensing process for foreign satellite to cable services coming into Canada, given a solid legislative base.
This is what Motion No. 36 seeks to do.
More important than this is Motion No. 39. This motion would ensure that with the exception of "three-plus-one", as I explained earlier, and border stations, the carriage of foreign signals should only be provided by cable systems if the programming they provide is complementary to that available from licensed Canadian broadcasters and network operators.
I admit that this motion is, in part, a response to the continuing penetration into the Canadian cable market by U.S. services. In particular I am referring to the recent decision to license U.S. superstations that provide the unique service of Beverly Hillbillies reruns 12 hours a day in addition to Atlanta Braves, Mets, and other baseball games.
As the producers' groups rightly said when they came before the legislative committee, "this will have a highly negative effect on Canadian producers to maintain a distinct Canadian market".
To quote Sam Jephcott again:
Canadian producers have relied on the "cordon sanitaire" that kept such channels out of Canada in the past, an advantage that allowed them to license original Canadian programming to Canadian broadcasters as well as American ones, without the diminution in value that inevitably occurs when market exclusivity is compromised by trans-border signal penetration.
That means that the American channels will come in and take over from our channels.
Just as important as the question of distinct Canadian production market is that of the viability of Canadian local stations, such as City TV in Toronto and specialty stations, in the face of competition from directly competing U.S. services.
As I noted earlier, this motion comes from a direct recommendation of the sixth report of the all-Party standing committee. Gerald Caplan and Florian Sauvageau warned against creating in effect a North American TV market, an idea which is embodied in this Bill. I quote: "If the rights to show American programs in Canada were retained and exploited by American broadcasters rather than being sold to Canadian broadcasters, it would be destructive to Canada's broadcasting system, particularly of private broadcasting. More importantly, it would create an even greater imbalance between foreign and Canadian programs, and reduce Canada's ability to produce such programs".
The Minister in her reply in debate said:
The prohibition of foreign radio and television services other than those whose programming is complementary to that available from Canadian broadcasters has not been included in the legislation, since it would unduly restrict Canadians' access to a range of international broadcasting services.
The impact of the Minister's policy is something different. I think the Minister is wrong. Her policy would limit Canadian choices and the chance to watch Canadian broadcasting services. As the Friends of Canadian Broadcasting rightly put it:
If this country had adopted such an approach 60 years ago this country would never have developed a separate Canadian broadcasting system except in the public sector.
I am not proposing to stop Canadians from getting complementary services. We just want Canadians to have the chance to provide them. The standing committee's sixth report, chaired by the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards) I believe, said:
We note that even in the large U.S. market, where service is provided entirely in English, there is only one available service in most programming categories. In Canada it is beyond question that a Canadian service could not co-exist with a non-Canadian service, especially if the Canadian service is expected to provide a meaningful contribution to Canadian programming.
I know that I have to wind up. I wonder if the House would bear with me for about one more minute. This is the most important element in the Bill.
There is a Conservative majority in this committee. What has made the Conservatives change their minds on this? We have to look at a group called The Cultural Industries Alliance, made up of more than a dozen major cultural organizations, which said the following:
We have already seen evidence of the effect of the trade agreement on existing policies and policy development. This includes the rejection of key recommendation for broadcast policy made by the House of Commons standing committee-
I think that this is the answer. The answer is that the Minister has no room to manoeuvre. She cannot manoeuvre


because of the trade deal and because of the Americanization of the North American market. That is why the standing committee reports were rejected, and that is why we are bringing forward these amendments.
If Canadian private broadcasting has to survive, I would hope that the Minister would accept it. If she wants it to survive in the future, in the face of this American competition, she should accept these amendments, at least the concept of complementary services.
Mr. Len Hopkins	(Renfrew-Nipissing

Pembroke):
Madam Speaker, I want to say a few words on Bill C-136, and in fact at the same time congratulate the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), from my own Party, who has been carrying the debate in committee and in the House of Commons so effectively.
Hear, hear!

She has indeed pointed out the great amount of evidence that exists that there is a tremendous liability to Canadian broadcasters in the future if this Bill is passed.
She has also brought out, very plainly, the fact that Canadian broadcasters will be very much under fire financially from the major television broadcasters in the United States under the trade deal. It is another example of how the trade deal can attack Canadian culture and will attack Canadian culture.
There must be a long-term look at this Bill. When you really take that long-term look, you realize the liability that exists therein for Canadian broadcasters. This is very clearly brought out in an article by Peter Mortimer of the Association of Canadian Film and Television Producers, who heads his article "Broadcast bill's flaws need fixing". He says that the legislation just would not do unless it is amended.
I am sure that the Minister is quite familiar with the comments contained therein.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: You are out of date. He has written again since.
She is talking now. I do not know whether or not she is agreeing with me.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: I was agreeing with Peter Mortimer's latest letter, the endorsement.

As the standing committee observed in its report, since Canadians receive television programming primarily by cable, the proportion of Canadian programming that cable offers is at least as important as the proportion of the programming offered by off-air broadcasters. Of course, we only need to take a look at the areas of Canadian life which Canadian television touches today to realize the percentage of
Broadcasting Act
the Canadian public that actually watch programs via cable television companies.
It concluded that the carriage regulations for cable are at least as important as the requirement for individual broadcasters in maintaining any reasonable balance between Canadians and foreign programming in the system. The task force and standing committee both concluded that broadcasting legislation should clearly define cable's role and give policy guidance to the CRTC regarding which channels cable television could carry. The standing committee recommended the following. The Bill should be drafted so as to define the central role of distribution undertakings-the cable systems- as that of distributing Canadian radio and television services in French and English, both public and private, with first priority given to public sector Canadian services followed by private Canadian services.
With the exception of the "three-plus-one" services that are very common to us, ABC, CBS, the NBC, and PBS already carried the bill and should make provision for the carriage of foreign radio and television services only when the programming they provide is complementary to that available from licensed Canadian broadcasters. For Canadian broadcasters to succeed they must be able to schedule the best foreign TV programs as well as Canadian programs. To the extent that directly competing American TV services become North American services, Canadian broadcasters' ability to buy attractive U.S. shows is eroded. If this happens, the value of rights that they manage to buy will be eroded by the lack of exclusivity. The Canadian Cable Television Association stated that it agreed in principle with this recommendation.
We are dealing here with professional people who have been in the cablevision business and television business for years. I think that their views should be taken absolutely seriously. They obviously have a few members of the committee. They have not been by most of the committee, and they have not as yet been taken seriously by the Government.
The Canadian Cable Television Association went on to suggest, however, that at the very least a cable subscriber should expect to receive every signal available off-air. The CRTC also stated that it agrees generally with this recommendation. It raised the same concern about border signals available off-air from the United States, although it noted that "the commission would agree that the spread of these nonCanadian services by means of microwave or satellite services should be discouraged".
The Government responded to this recommendation in Bill C-136 by avoiding the issue. Instead of offering guidance on how the CRTC should treat the carriage of foreign services, the Bill simply states that distribution undertakings should accord priority to the carriage of Canadian programming services. That is contained in subclause 3(1 )(q) (i). In other words, as long as licensed Canadian services are carried, all American stations and networks can also be carried.


Broadcasting Act
By explicitly favouring the carriage of conventional pay and specialty American television services that compete directly with licensed Canadian services, the Government has hidden its head in the sand on the implications this policy has for the existence of a separate Canadian broadcasting market. To the extent that conventional U.S. stations and networks come in to Canada they erode the value of Canadian rights. One can readily see that because of the massive, unbalanced distribution of signals and television companies on each side of the border and the wealth contained therein.
In the case of the United States pay and specialty services, such rights will not be available to Canadian broadcasters at all. Having introduced legislation to ensure a separate distribution market in Canada for film and video products, the Government is clearly unwilling to see the erosion of the separate markets that have traditionally existed for broadcasting programs.
Having addressed that in general terms, I would now like to move an amendments:
That Motion No. 37 be amended by adding at the end of subparagraph (ii) and subparagraph (iii) the words:
"under terms and conditions set out by the Commission",
These words would simply be added on to Motion No. 37 after subparagraphs (ii) and (iii). The motion is seconded by the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer (Mr. Isabelle).

speechtext: I agree. Tell the CRTC.
Well, it is the CRTC. However, sometimes the CRTC can be wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: Absolutely.

It allowed Videon Cable to offer three more choices on its channel. The customers who buy the services provided by Videon Cable were not asked if they wanted an increase in the number of channels to which they could tune in. They certainly were not asked if they wanted the three that were added. In fact, not a single person who has called me agrees with those three channels, and the monthly bill was increased by 91 cents. It is time to have a careful look at the whole situation of the cable companies.
Almost every person and every group involved in television has opposed the expansion of rights that the Government is giving to the cable companies in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: That is the CRTC.

Our position is the position brought forward in the Caplan-Sauvageau report and in the task force report. I wish to quote a couple of sentences from the report of the House of Commons standing committee on this question. In indicating why it did not like this idea, it stated: "There would be incentives to market the vertically integrated service in competition or to the detriment of independently owned pay or specialty services, and will lead to a further fracturing of the market for existing companies".
Therefore our position is supported by the Caplan-Sauvageau Commission, the task report, and in the briefs presented to the legislative committee which argued that content should be kept separate from carriage. We see the cable industry as


being like Bell Canada in the transmission business, They should be subject, like Bell, to rate of return regulation. It has been suggested that one of the main reasons the cable industry wants to become involved in programming is to blur further its status as a carrier. If any Government were to come to them and attempt to make the cable industry subject to such regulation, we will have the CCTA come before us and say: "We are different from Bell and we are basically a programming undertaking", and so on.
We oppose the further expansion of the cable companies and the services they supply, and the ability it will give them to increase the rate of profits which, in our opinion, are already much too great for the cable companies.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to speak to the subamendment and say, first of all, that I would have no trouble voting in favour of this provision because I believe it would provide a firm direction for the main amendment, Motion No. 37 now before the House.
I may recall Motion No. 37 to amend Bill C-136 in Clause 3, which adds the following:
"(i) should accord priority to the carriage of Canadian programming services, in French and English, both public and private, with priority given to the Canadian public element programming services,
(ii)	may carry foreign originated programming services only where the programming they provide is substantially different from that already offered by a licensed Canadian broadcasting undertaking or where those foreign programming services were already carried by distribution undertakings,
(iii)	should be regulated in a manner that reflects a reasonable recognition of exclusive rights acquired by Canadian broadcasting undertakings,".

In speaking to these three points under the subamendment, I would like to make it clear that in ten minutes one cannot do justice to all the thoughts and points one would like to raise. I would like to talk about the parliamentary network and the recent shuffling of the parliamentary channel on cable. In my riding, for example, and I know the Speaker has received lots of letters and will be receiving more on this subject, there is quite a bit of unease about the fact that some cable companies have "elevated" the parliamentary channel so that many people who were receiving it cannot receive it any more unless they have a special hook-up. That hook-up is costly, I think $100.
In an article written on the weekend by John Warren, there is reference to a 1986 survey by Environics Research which shows that 3 per cent of all Canadians tune in, almost daily, to the parliamentary channel. Another 10 per cent watch it at least once a week. The numbers are 750,000 people daily with an additional 2.5 million each week. If their situation is like that of people in my riding where Skyline has moved it from Channel 16 to Channel 50, they are just out of luck. They
Broadcasting Act
cannot hear me anymore because someone made a decision to put other stations ahead of the parliamentary channel. I find that a bit difficult to accept, and I would like to tell the CRTC that indeed I expect that if this amendment is approved they will accord priority to a channel of such importance as the parliamentary channel.
We had the pleasure today of welcoming the British select committee on televising proceedings of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom. Maybe they would like to hear from some of us about what we feel about this broadcasting. Maybe they would like to hear from Canadians about how they feel about receiving the signal. I know I was quite impressed with the decision when it was taken some 11 years ago in this House. I was not too sure it was going to be very well received, but I am amazed to see how many people in my riding of Ottawa-Vanier come up to me every week and say: "I saw you on TV this week". I say: "What was I saying?" "I don't know but I saw you on TV".

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: Is that good or bad?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The fact that they see you there is very important to people. I hope they understand I am trying to fight to get this channel back into the basic service so that people at home can receive the parliamentary channel.
The second point I want to make concerning according priority to the carriage of Canadian programming services in French and English, both public and private, is the famous question I raised this morning about TV-5.

I would like to get back to that, Madam Speaker, because TV-5 is important to French-speaking Canadians. I would like to give an overview of the present situation since 1 said this morning that people living outside Quebec have to pay more to receive the TV-5 signal, and that is quite true. It costs almost $6 more to receive the TV5 signal if you live outside Quebec.
The Association des cablodistributeurs du Quebec has signed an agreement with the Quebec-Canada television consortium under which cable distributors may transmit the signal to all subscribers to their basic service at a cost of, get this, $1.63 per month, which includes TV-5, Canal Famille, Meteo Media, Musique Plus and YTV. YTV is an English station which I watched at home not long ago, and I thought their programs were quite interesting.
Unfortunately, in provinces outside Quebec, for instance here in Ontario, negotiations did not lead to this kind of agreement. Here in Ottawa, as I said this morning, subscribers to Skyline Cablevision can receive TV-5 and Canal Famille- two channels, which is half the number Quebec viewers can receive-and they have to pay $2 per month more, while it takes another $4 to rent the decoder to be able to receive the signal. So it costs them $6 to get half the services that are available to Quebecers for $1.63.


Broadcasting Act
Madam Speaker, I find that hard to swallow. We are not any richer over here. We are not asking for more. We just want the same kind of deal they are getting in Quebec. Under the agreement between the Association des cablodistributeurs du Quebec and the Quebec-Canada television consortium, cable distributors, get this, can buy the signal at a cost of 29 cents per subscriber for the first year. To these costs should, of course, be added the cost of equipment depreciation and administrative costs, all of which are included in the $1.63 charge to Quebec subscribers. As for cable distributors outside Quebec, everything depends on the agreements which, I hope, will be signed some day by TV-5 with each distibutor. As I see it, considering the national investment in setting up the TV-5 network, and the fact that as Canadians we have invested millions to make this programming available to Canadians as part of a cultural mission and a desire to achieve a linguistic balance, 1 think equity should be restored as soon as possible in this respect.
I would therefore ask the Government and the CRTC- because I think the Minister is well aware of the problem, and she let me know she would try to push the CRTC to make this a priority-to put before the Canadian public a list of criteria that cable distributors should meet. That is in fact the purpose, as I see it, of item 1, the purpose we are trying to explain to Canadians, which is to accord priority to the carriage of Canadian programming services, in French and English, both public and private, with priority given to the Canadian public element programming services. That is all we are trying to do, Madam Speaker, and I hope the amendment and subamendment will be accepted.
In item 2, and I want to read it, "may carry foreign ordinary programming services only when the program they provide is substantially different". We are trying to grandfather the existing 22 foreign services, if I may use those words. I guess I would have to say that American programming is actually in the basic service right now. In support of this amendment I quote the Association of Canadian Film and Television Producers that stated the following in a publication:
With the exception of the "three-plus-one" services (ABC, CBS, NBC and PBS) already carried, the Act should make provision for the carriage of foreign radio and television services only when the programming they provide is complementary to that available from licensed Canadian broadcasters.
I see that I should wrap up my comments, Madam Speaker. I want to tell the House that what we are trying to do here is to strengthen the legislation, to make it a little more responsive, to get the CRTC to move, and to get the priorities set.

Madam
Speaker, I believe I can speak again on the subamendment, the amendment to the amendment. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) raised some very interesting
points about which we sometimes lose track when we are debating technicalities.
Cable companies, however, have incredible power. Recently there has been a switch of channels and people are very upset. Not only are people facing increased prices for cable-

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: It is the CRTC.

I know the CRTC makes the rulings, but on the application of the cable companies.
If you give the cable companies, as this Bill is doing, the power to broadcast, to originate programming, if you like, other than local programming, regular programming-and they are the ones that carry the transmission-you have a potential conflict of interest, Madam Speaker. As someone pointed out, the potential for conflict is great as demonstrated when used to promote Canadian pay services taken over by cable's own Home Shopping Club Network.
In its sixth report the standing committee, chaired by a Conservative Member, gave the following examples of the danger of what it called vertical integration. Let me quote from it:
-the allocation of revenue between the distribution undertaking and the network operator directly affects the capacity of the network operator to meet its Canadian content and other programming obligations.
If distribution undertakings are permitted to own and operate such programming services, they would in effect be negotiating affiliation agreements with themselves, and would have an incentive to maximize the allocation of revenue to the distribution function. Moreover, there would be incentives to market the vertically integrated service in competition with or to the detriment of independently owned pay or specialty services.
The Hon. Member from Winnipeg suggested that a number of groups opposed this but the Minister said: "No, they do not any more". These groups have consistently opposed allowing cable to originate broadcasting. I do not know where cable got all this influence with the Government, but the cable companies are the big winners in this Bill, and there is a potential for conflict.
Here is what Gary Neil of ACTRA, the union, summarized when he appeared before the committee:
There are two aspects to the production of programming by cable. At the moment they are involved to some extent through the community channel and we do not think it is inappropriate and would not be particularly concerned if this bill were recognizing that in law.
In other words, you recognize that they can program with the community channel. He continued:
However when you get to a more general question of them originating programming, the difficulty with vertical integration is that the individuals making decisions about what will be available to Canadians would also have produced some of the material available for distribution.
Not all of the material, but some of it. He went on to say:
Clearly there will be prejudice on their part to decide in favour of the materials they have produced. It is a conflict of interest.
Michelle D'Auray of the Canadian Conference of the Arts said:


We do not believe a cable operator licensed as a carrier should be a programmer, doing content, because the concentration of ownership we already see elements of, would allow for too much control over the system for one company, one corporation. We also believe the system has been built on the distinction of carrier and content and should be maintained at that level.

The Association des producteurs de films et de videos du Quebec said this: We see to our dismay that the legislator ignored the recommendation in the Sauvageau-Caplan Report and preferred to authorize distributors to be involved in programming for local or other needs.

Our position is that content should be kept separate from carriage. We see the cable industry as being like Bell Canada in the transmission business. It should be subject, like Bell, to a regulated rate of return. The cable industry is making a tremendous rate of return, some say over 50 per cent. We feel that one of the reasons the cable industry wants to get involved in programming is that it would blur its status as a carrier. If any future Government were to come to it and attempt to make the cable industry subject to such regulation, like Bell as a carrier, it would come before the Minister and say: "We are different from Bell because we program as well as carry." We think that is the inarticulated major premise why the cable industry wanted in this Bill as a programmer and is what it won from the Government. I do not know what the price the Conservatives will pay for it but they have certainly given a huge favour to the cable industry, the one group that always supported the Bill.
These amendments attempt to stop the Government from mixing content and carriage. Let me quote Mr. Andrew Roman of the Public Interest Advocacy Centre when he discussed that danger:
-it will not be long before you are going to start to see the cable industry wanting to program channels and wanting to accept advertising, and seeking exemptions from certain classes of regulations from the CRTC or the Cabinet and going head to head with broadcasters.
If they can do that, because of the inherent advantage they have with the technology because they control the delivery system for 60 per cent or 65 per cent of Canadian households, they can put every broadcaster today out of business if they want to, just by grabbing up their advertising revenues and by using the same program producers on a contract basis as virtually everybody else does.
Look out, here comes Ted Rogers and the rest of the cable people to take over the private broadcasting in the long run in Canada or at the minimum to avoid their huge profits from being regulated. That is what is behind this.
I invite the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards) to speak. As I understand his sixth committee report, it said that there should be a distinction between carriage and content. Is he still holding that position?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that some of what we have been hearing in the debate today relates to ideology and not to principle. I challenge the Hon. Member to tell the House whether or not it is the official policy of the New

Madam Speaker, the new Parliamentary Secretary is very able in slipping in a bon mot.
We are addressing a whole distribution system. Subclause 3(r) relates to distribution undertakings. We have to realize that we are facing a new structure, a new option or a new right, whichever way we put it, that the Government has accorded to the cable industry. I will not argue with the Government's right to make those decisions. It has decided that the distribution undertakings can be concerned with both content and carriage, but I would ask the Minister if she would please seriously consider this.
There already is serious fragmentation of the base and tremendous competitiveness in the broadcasting industry with the networks, the programming undertakings and the broadcast undertakings now having the right to be programmers. Perhaps the Minister would at least consider containing their rights in this particular area to programming that would be complementary. It is in that regard that I had moved Motion No. 41. I would be very pleased if she would look at that particular motion and give some serious consideration to it.
When local broadcasters will be in competition with local distribution undertakings, it will set up a very difficult situation. The viability of those individual broadcasters may well be challenged.
What I consider one of the most fundamental aspects of this Bill, and one of the most fundamental principles that needs to be integrated into this Bill so that the Broadcasting Act effectively responds to a Canadian system, is Canadian content and Canadian realities. I would plead with the Minister to look very carefully at Motion No. 37. I suggest to the Minister that it is consistent with the view of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. It was supported by the CRTC and, believe it or not, by the cable people.
The limiting of the carrying of foreign programming services is seen as detrimental to our system. I have, in my motion, grandfathered that which already exists. I feel strongly that we ought not add any additional American services until we have enabled our own Canadian services to grow and to reflect what we believe to be in the best interests of the Canadian broadcasting system.


Broadcasting Act
The standing committee recommended the prohibition of further carriage of foreign programming in its fifteenth report, and this was made quite clear in recommendations 139, 140, 141, and 142. The Minister answered this by saying that the prohibition of foreign radio and television services other than those whose programming is complementary to that available from Canadian broadcasters has not been included in the legislation since it would unduly restrict the access of Canadians to a range of international broadcasting services.
I would suggest that we in Canada are far from being discriminated against. Certainly our access to foreign services is not restricted. I would remind the Minister that because of our good-neighbour policy and because of the airwaves that flow over the border, 71 per cent of all the television programs viewed by English-speaking Canadians are American. I would remind her that 80 per cent of our publishing industry is in foreign hands, 97 per cent of films shown in Canada are foreign, and 85 per cent of records and tapes sold in Canada are based on imported master tapes. The thrust is to change that reality and enable us to have our own industries.
I think it is important that Canadian broadcasters have some exclusivity of rights. One of the things my amendment does is provide that the Canadian broadcasting system be regulated in a manner that recognizes exclusive rights of broadcasters. It would also, I think, enable the essential role of the distribution undertakings, the distributing of Canadian radio and television services in English and in French, both public and private. The first priority would be given to the public sector. Canadian services including specialty services would be clearly defined so that the CRTC could not in any way avoid the responsibilities which we believe it should have. Only if it has a clear direction in the legislation can it then be held responsible if it does not follow the will expressed in the Bill.
The Standing Committee said that this was very important. It is just as appropriate and important to establish a basis for requiring the licensed broadcasters to give priority to carrying Canadian programs and it is at least as important to establish a legislative base that requires that distribution undertakings give priority to carrying Canadian undertakings.
I was glad my colleague from Vanier talked about the place of the House of Commons channel. It is disappearing very far up the dial. In fact, I just spoke to an elderly aunt of mine. She tells me that she cannot get it because she has an MATV system which does not bring it in. My mother-in-law cannot get it because she does not have a converter that goes that high. Perhaps they have been saved from this unbelievable debate. Nevertheless, if this priority carriage was there, public and private Canadian services could be on basic services and these people could get access to those services.
I would suggest that we must limit foreign programming. It is absolutely fundamental. Rather than allowing the Americans to invade, I would suggest we could occasionally learn some lessons from them.
It is interesting to note that on May 18, 1988, this year, the United States Federal Communications Commission decided to reimpose a requirement which it had removed in 1980, that cable systems in the United States not import a distant broadcasting signal-that is about 32 miles or something like that-even when done on a compulsory license basis, whenever a program contained in that signal has been acquired for exclusive use by a local broadcaster. This rule is one from which we could learn and it would help Canadian broadcasters to have Canadian rights that would not be diluted by having their programs shown on Sunday while the other programs are shown on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday without simultaneous substitution. It will enable them to have a decent financing base from the advertising revenue.
The last point is that in the limiting of foreign program carriage, I would suggest we would end up, as I have indicated in my amendments, grandfathering the 17 presently accepted American programs and the 5 new ones that have been accorded as a result of the November, 1987 hearings. Thus we would limit the damage being done by this overwhelming presence which is eroding the program rights and the revenue base of our own Canadian broadcasters. I would like to see them have the exclusive rights which they buy right across the system and let us separate out our markets so we know that we have a Canadian broadcasting system that reflects Canada.

Madam Speaker, in this group of amendments, there are several subgroups that I would just like to comment on. The first is with regard to Motion No. 33 which deals with the proposals put forward in the legislation for an alternative programmer which the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) would take out.
We have heard a lot said in the House about Canadian content and and about the need for more Canadian content. Nothing will bring more variety of Canadian content whether from our multicultural communities or dealing with the regional nature of our country, the diversity of our country, or the arts and the culture of our country, than an alternative programming service. It has been argued for time and again by the Caplan-Sauvageau task force and by many, many others.
I would like to read an extract from a letter at which I had just been looking at as I was listening to the discussion. It is from the Dean of the Faculty of Fine Arts at the University of Calgary. He says:
Needless to say I am absolutely delighted that there is provision in the proposed new broadcasting act for a new service that will pay attention not only to the multicultural realities of Canada but also to the vast storehouse of talent concerned with the arts. I believe unless the arts can find a place in the Canadian broadcasting system they are in danger of becoming irrelevant to succeeding generations of Canadians.
I mention that because this new service will offer, over and above what is now there, an additional outlet for our many Canadian creative talents: artists, composers, and so many people in that field. I would ask the Hon. Member to reconsider her position. The rules that would govern this are that the


CRTC would hold hearings and that there would be input from groups all across the country in order to construct the best possible alternative programming service that we could have. We have asked only that it be ready to go on air within two years' time. I think that can be met. There have been many expressions of interest already made to us by people who want to see that come about.
The second group of amendments to which I want to speak is this key one with regard to the licensing of U.S. services. I have heard what Members have to say about this. I want to state specifically why we have gone the route that we have, in fact giving the responsibility and the power to a Canadian regulatory body to determine what is accepted on cable and what is not.
In fact, the CRTC itself regulates the introduction of U.S. services by permitting only those services that are complementary to Canadian domestic services. The CRTC is the gatekeeper. I have heard arguments put forward saying that we should really license all of these, whether they are off-air or whether they are by cable. The Hon. Member for Mount Royal said that she would grandfather certain ones. Well, that really is not a logical position because if you are going to ask for the licensing of one service from the United States, surely you should be consistent and ask for the licensing of all services.
I just want to ask the Members who have put forward these proposals whether or not they have considered what this would mean. I am very concerned and very serious about this because it is true, I suppose, that we could ask, we could determine, we could demand, that every U.S. service coming into this country be licensed under Canadian regulations, whether it happens to be HBO or ABC.
One of the key criteria about Canadian licensing regulations is that the Canadian distribution service and the Canadian broadcaster be 80 per cent owned in this country. That being the case, how would you ask HBO, ABC, NBC, or anything else to be 80 per cent Canadian owned and controlled in order to have a Canadian licence? I suppose the only way you could do it is by weakening the content or the requirements under Canadian licensing, that is, to less than 80 per cent Canadian controlled. However, we are not prepared to do that with regard to those systems which are licensed in this country. They must remain Canadian owned and controlled.
Therefore we ask how we then guard against the proliferation of a great many services coming into this country from outside. We do it through the regulatory body that we have established in this country, the CRTC, and by requiring that the CRTC tell the cable distributors that they must ensure that only those services that are complementary to what is being offered here are carried. In that way you have some means of control, but if we lose that control anything could be acceptable.
Broadcasting Act
That is an argument that I want opposition Members to think very carefully about because, while what they are suggesting may sound good in the heat of the moment, if they really examine where it would lead us, they will find that it is not where they really want to be.
I feel that the authority and the power should be given to a Canadian regulatory body to determine what comes into this country. Look at some of the things which, even under the existing Act-and under the new Act it will be stronger-have been licensed and some of the things which have not been licensed. For instance, our cable services carry First Choice but they do not carry HBO. They carry The Sports Network but not ESPN. They carry Much Music, not MTV.
The CRTC looks at this and sees what is complementary. It is for that reason that we will put the requirement on the CRTC to decide what services cable carries and what they do not, and why they must maintain a larger balance of Canadian services than American. That is what you will see if you look at the division even in the present set-up.
The third area I want to mention briefly is the comments that have been made with regard to the cable programming role and whether or not they should be into programming as well as into carriage. There has been a lot of discussion about this. I think it is important to note that cable is already into programming. There have been a lot of services through community channels and through the Youth Television Network which have already been authorized by the CRTC. It is not as if this was something new.
We have written into this Bill very strict requirements with regard to programming as undertaken by cable. Yes, going that route was a very conscious policy decision on the part of the Government, but we ensured that the possibility of a conflict of interest arising when distributors originate programming was addressed by putting in two sections, with which I am sure the cable industry is not very happy, to ensure that the programming is properly monitored and properly produced. I am referring, of course, to Subclauses 9(l)(h) and 10(l)(h) of the Bill. We have put in these controls so that the conflict of interest possibilities are lessened, indeed regulated.
It is for these reasons, Madam Speaker, that I wanted to interject in the debate at this point. I wanted to explain why we are doing the things we are doing. We think that in the long run they will be better. We think that having the CRTC as the gatekeeper for programming is better than even considering the possibility in any way of lessening the demands of Canadian ownership and control. We think that there is a role for cable.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) mentioned the moneys that cable companies earn. I want to see that money reinvested in Canadian programming. In the way in which the Bill is written, that requirement to meet Canadian content applies to cable companies ordistribu-tion undertakings as it does on to programming of the CBC.


Broadcasting Act
It has to apply to all sections of the broadcasting industry and not just to isolated parts of it, as it had in the past.

Motion No. 45

She said: Madam Speaker, we are talking in this group, first, about the definition of "network", which I would like to look at and discuss with the Minister. I proposed an amendment which I hoped she will find favour with. The second is a full amendment under Motion No. 47, which is a deletion of


Clause 5(2) of the cable regulations and supervision of the system, and the consequential amendments which would flow from that on Motions Nos. 44, 46, and 50. Actually, Motion No. 44 would add the place of the CRTC within the broadcasting system into Clause 3, which is the broadcastng policy.
I would just like to start by addressing the question of networks. We talked for a long time of services, which are available in an increasing number of Canadian households, that operate without a licence and earn revenue from Canada without any obligation to contribute to the Canadian programming system. It is of concern. It was an ongoing concern of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
In the prior set of amendments we were addressing the 17 American networks or superstations which had been accorded access to Canada through Canadian cable regulations, in essence. This amendment which I am proposing would in a sense stop the Americanization of our television system and create a better playing field, if I may use that rather overused term.
I would like to suggest that in the course of the amendment which I am going to bring on networking, the licensed Canadian services operating on the same basis that they presently work must spend money on Canadian programs and offer a balance of Canadian and non-Canadian programs. Therefore we have a sense of double standards. We have loose ends out there. We have a direct broadcast satellite service that is not properly covered-its signals are not covered-and pay per view has a potential of coming in here. I am suggesting that rules should be the same for everyone, and that the definition of networks should apply to satellite and cable services.
I would like to remind the Minister that even the CCTA endorsed the concept in the July, 1987 brief, and I refer to page 10 of that brief.
I had some legal advice which I would like to share with the Minister. When we look at the purposes of Clause 5(2), where the Minister refers to the services that carry on in whole or in part within Canada, it includes the transmission of a broadcasting service wherever it may be originated to a member of the public in Canada, directly or indirectly, where such transmission involves a contractual relationship with a member of the public or with a distribution undertaking serving a member of the public.
In that amendment which I am proposing I would like to suggest to the Minister that it implements recommendation 17 of the sixth report of our standing committee. Although the Minister made certain responses about the fact that she cannot cover services that do not have a business presence in Canada and operate under American law, she considers that it is doubtful whether it would be legally possible to require these services to submit to licensing by the CRTC, because Canada-did I say something wrong; sorry-cannot extend its laws beyond its territory.
Broadcasting Act
I would like to suggest to the Minister that this comment is based on a misconception of fact and on an error in law. The misconception is that the recommendation would apply to off-air U.S. border stations. These stations do not contract to deliver these services to members of the public in Canada, and it is not captured through the nature of the amendment which I am proposing.
The principal focus of the recommendation is on the U.S. speciality networks, like Arts and Entertainment, CNN, et cetera, which enter into contracts with Canadian cable systems in Canada to deliver their service to Canadian homes. This activity is clearly capable of falling under Canadian law if legislatures wish it to, and if this be the case.
The term "undertaking" does not require actual physical presence or physical assets to be present in Canada. A number of cases have held that the mere presence of a signal in Canada can give rise to tortious-a marvellous legal word, the Minister does not know that I looked up her definition too-or copyright liability. I would suggest that her staff refer to Jenner v. Sun Oil (1952), or to CAPAC v. International Good Music (1963).
The wording proposed would also cover pay per view and direct broadcast satellite operations, offering their services to Canadians, to the extent that the services delivered on a contracted basis. In practical terms this confines the ambit of the clause to incrypted signals, where the signal originator authorizes a Canadian home to decode the signal for a fee. The committee certainly heard about how this is often sold under the table and illegally.
The fact that the United States service may not have a business presence in Canada does not preclude the Government from taking steps against the marketers or distributors of the service who generally operate in Canada. Making the legislation effective raises the same practical problems as going after illegal lottery operators or boiler room operations, operating over the border by telephone. You prosecute any local intermediary, issue stop mail orders, or take other quasicriminal steps available in Canada.
The proposed amendment does not actually prohibit U.S. services from operating in Canada. However, it would require them to obtain a CRTC licence for the first time.
In order to make room for complementary U.S. specialty services, it is expected that the direction on Canadian ownership would have to be amended to permit such services to qualify for licences. However, under Clause 9(2), that exemption could certainly take place, or under a broad policy directive. Such licences would presumably be issued for a transitional period only, so that would-be Canadian services in the same program category would not be foreclosed from applying or eventually operating in Canada with a Canadian version of the U.S. service, often even more interesting. We do not allow-and the Minister alluded to this a little earlier- HBO or ESPN, because we have First Choice and TSN.


Broadcasting Act
I would suggest that this whole thought of complementary versus competition in access to Canadian networks, to the Canadian little box where you punch buttons and you get what you want to see, is very key to the effective operation of this Bill. As the presence in Canada of American exports expands, and they take more and more money out of our market, we must find ways to be concerned about Americanization and take some kind of control over what is going on.
There has been an all-Party agreement in committee. If the cable industry was not so concerned, and it agreed, I would like to know why the Minister cannot agree to this particular motion. I strongly ask the Minister to give it serious consideration.
With respect to Motion Nos. 44, 46, 47, and 50, one of the elements in this Bill is Clause 5(2) which sets forth a number of objectives for the regulation and supervision of the broadcasting system. These are intended to be distinct from the objectives of the broadcasting policy set forth in Clause 3(1). Clause 5(3) states that the objectives for the regulation and supervision of the system set out in subclause (2) rank lower in priority to any conflicting objections in Clause 3(1). I would like to suggest to the Minister that there needs to be degree of clarity here. I have made what I hope the Minister will find, upon consultation, an amendment which can be helpful.
A review of the objectives stipulated in subclause 5(2) shows that four out of the six subclauses are largely duplicative and are of concepts already recognized in Clause 3(1). In particular Clause 5(2)(a) is the same as Clause 3(l)(b). Clause 5(2)(b) is the same as Clause 3(1 )(h)(ii). Clause 5(2)(c) is the same as Clause 3(l)(c)(iv), and Clause 5(2)(d) is a watered down version of Clause 3(l)(i). As a result, I believe that it will be confusing and it will be ill-fitting to reiterate those concepts (a) to (d) in Clause 5(2). Therefore, my Motion No. 47 flows from that thought. It deletes the articles in Clause 2. It would leave only Clause 5(2)(e) and Clause 5(2)(f) unaccounted for, and they are genuinely important and represent new concepts in the Bill. I recommend that they be moved to Clause 3, which is the over-all broadcasting policy, and can effectively indicate the role, place, and importance of the CRTC in the over-all broadcasting policy for Canada. I have added only one word, which would be to add the "Canadian" dimension to the role to be played by the CRTC.
In summation, I suggest that Clauses 5(2)(e) and (f) would now be placed under general broadcast policy as a new Clause 3(1 )(s) while at the same time adding that Canadian dimension. If all that is taken into consideration, I believe that we would avoid conflict between the objectives and the supervision of the system, and add a degree of clarity which I hope the Minister would find favourable. I would suggest that the CRTC also agrees with that perspective. I hope the Minister will see fit to give serious consideration to accepting the amendments.

Madam Speaker, on behalf of the NDP, it is true that many of the subclauses of Clause 5(2) are similar to Clause 3. We have taken a slightly different position than that taken by my colleague from the Liberal Party on this matter. We see Clause 5 as potentially serving a useful role. We have proposed some amendments which will be coming up in the next round of motions. If Clause 5(2) can be improved, we would probably support that clause.
We do support Motion No. 50 moved by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal. It is exactly the same as Motion No. 51 which I proposed. After a good deal of thought and discussion in the legislative committee, I have come to a position which is pretty close to that of the Minister with respect to the powers of the CRTC, as well as its decision-making process. Indeed, as I recall, the Minister accepted one of my amendments on this subject in committee. However, I believe that some refinements are still in order, and I believe that Motion No. 50 is one of them.
It would allow the broad power of policy direction to apply relative to Clause 3(1), the broadcasting policy for Canada. However, it would take away from the Government the power to make direction under Clause 5(2). I believe this would improve this section of the Bill by allowing the commission to act more independently, while at the same time maintaining the general power of policy direction by the Government. I urge the Minister to support Motion No. 50.
