BALANCING OF BUDGET Mr. Joe Reid (St. Catharines) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Constitution of Canada so as to require the government to submit a balanced budget except:
(a)	in times of a declared national emergency or disaster, or
(b)	if the deficit receives parliamentary approval by a two-thirds majority.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is an honour and privilege to rise on Motion M-151 to put to the House and Canadians an idea that I believe is essential to the future and the long-term stability of our country as a nation and as a society.
The basic principle of the motion requires a constitutional amendment that would require governments to balance the budgets we present here in Parliament. I have listed three exceptions. One is a declared national emergency. Another is a declared national disaster. The third is if this Parliament, by a vote of two-thirds of its Members, declares in favour of a deficit. I hasten to reassure Members that I am not wedded to the specific wording of the basic principle or the exceptions. There may well be other exceptions that Members come up with that we would all find acceptable. Perhaps a two-thirds majority is too high. However, it seems to me as parliamentarians our prime concern has to be for the long-term future and stability of our country.
We entrench in our Constitution our democratic rights because we know we cannot trust power solely to people. We also entrench human rights. I certainly would be prepared to work with other Members to work up a constitutional amendment that would protect future generations from environmental breaches. We need environmental protection in our Constitution for future generations. However, the purpose of this debate is constitutional protection for future generations on economic matters.
Why am I concerned? This year the deficit will be some $28 billion. Members know that a mere four years ago it was $38 billion. Certainly it is being reduced each year and that is a step in the right direction, but on April 1 of every year the deficit is moved over to the national debt. Members will remember that in 1968 the national debt was some $18 billion, even though we had built this country, fought two world wars, and endured 10 years of depression. However, since 1968, as a result of succeeding government budget deficits, the national debt has gone up to over $300 billion. The cost of servicing that debt is something like $31 billion or $32 billion. That is at current interest rates. We remember that three short years ago interest rates were 23 per cent. That would mean over $60 billion coming right off the top just to service the debt. I firmly believe that would lead to instability and rash action which could impair the future of our country. Certainly it would affect the well being of future generations.
As you well know, the national debt is simply excess spending on ourselves. Yet it has to be paid for by someone. If we do not, it will be put off into the future and our children and grandchildren will pay it. That will be done either through increased taxes or they will receive far fewer services. Or, some future Government will simply turn on the printing presses and we know what that does. We just need to look at all the Third World countries which have a small group of people who are fabulously rich and a mass of poor people. When you look at their economic history, every one has had a government which turned on the printing press and paid their national debt in that way. However, that leads to inflation, high interest rates and collapse. Surely none of us would individually impose that on our children or our grandchildren. Yet collectively since 1968 we have run our national debt from $18 billion to over $300 billion.


What I am saying, and I would like to hear other Members' views, is that it has got so bad that we now need a constitutional amendment that will protect our children and grandchildren from us. That is a terrible thing to say, but the fact is that representative parliamentary democracy has developed to the point in this country and others, particularly in the western world, where the interest groups are so powerful that they are able to convince Parliament to override the broad general interest of the country as a whole. We can all list examples of special interest groups which have received special concessions in this and past Parliaments. They were probably not in the national interest in the long-term, and if we had an entrenched constitutional amendment we would be protected from those types of pressures and powers.
Clearly, I want Canadians to appreciate the magnificent job done by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Today we spend about $100 billion on programs such as health care and defence and we are taxing away from Canadians about $103 billion. Therefore, we have a surplus of some $3 billion, yet we have a deficit of $28 billion. The reason is that we have to take about $31 billion right off the top to pay to people who have lent money to the Government.
Who are those people? They have more money than they are using at the moment, so they lend it to the Government. If you had $1 million you would never go out and put it in the business. You would lend it to your own Government where it is absolutely guaranteed, particularly as interest rates go up. That is what happened during the late 1970s, and it is not good for the country or our children.
Just imagine if past Governments had done what the Minister of Finance is doing in producing a balanced budget or indeed a surplus. We would not have a national debt. Think of what we could do in health care. Think of what we could do in research and development at a time when the nation needs to have research and development. We are on the cutting edge in competition with other countries. Just think of what we would be able to do for young women who in our society today have to work and choose an abortion for economic reasons rather than keeping a child.
Because of interest on the national debt, we today are beginning to lose opportunities. I think that is very bad. I wish I could have a full 20 minutes because there are many other points I would like to make, but I am anxious to hear from my colleagues. I hope in due course, if not in this Parliament but perhaps as a result of the debate here today that we will be able to refine the motion and in the next Parliament it will be resubmitted by myself if I happen to be successful in the election or by some other Member, and over a period of years this idea will grow to fruition. I hope within my own lifetime it will lead to the entrenchment of economic protection for future generations against our excesses as a result of the state of our democracy today.
Constitution of Canada

Mr. Speaker,
I am always surprised to hear Tory Members discussing the deficit. In 1984 we on this side of the House, particularly myself, took a very firm position on that during the campaign.
I must say that Tory Members also took a position on the deficit. I suggest it was a normal course of action, particularly after the economic crisis that we had here in Canada. The former Liberal Government had to do something to support the unemployed by developing special programs to create jobs, otherwise the rate of employment would have been larger and small business people would have lost a greater part of their market, resulting in more difficulties for Canadian workers.
After having heard speeches, particularly from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), we expected something important from the Tory Government, but what we saw was in direct contradiction to what was said. Both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance said publicly, and repeated during the 1984 campaign, that they would cut the deficit but would never increase taxes. The Government has done exactly the opposite. The Government did not cut spending in terms of inflation, but has increased taxes to the tune of $26 billion. In the actual fiscal year that represents $11 billion, but if we take into account the positive effect of fiscal reform, it amounts to a net $9 billion in new taxes, not because of the growth in the economy but because of tax increases, sales tax, gasoline tax, personal income tax and so on.
I guess the Member is expressing the Tory point of view. He is coming back with the same rhetoric as before. In other words he is saying "we have to cut the deficit". He is proposing to put in the Canadian Constitution that, except in very difficult situations, we should not have a deficit at all.
It is very nice to hear those kinds of speeches a few weeks before the writ is dropped and before the election, but it is another thing to deliver the goods. After six years of economic recovery, where have the Tory Members been while we have had tax increases and big deficits year after year? That is two more years than the number of years the Tories have been in power. The recovery started two years before the Tory election in 1984. They voted for tax reform. When the Minister made his speech, they applauded him. Where were they when the deficit was still $28 billion or $29 billion after six years of economic recovery? They were no place at all. They did not raise any questions. After the damage has been done and after the Tory Government has added an almost 60 per cent increase to the national debt, we are presented with a motion for a change to the Canadian Constitution to eliminate the deficit. But where were they during that actual debate?
I read in the the Toronto Star about the series of promises which the Prime Minister and other Ministers have made. They add up to more than $14 billion. Where were you, Sir, when all those announcements were made?

Are you for or against it?


Constitution of Canada

These will increase the deficit. We hear the Prime Minister saying that the environment is becoming the main priority for the Tories in the coming election, but where are the Members? They probably discussed the matter in caucus because they will have to increase the environmental budget which was cut by the Tories themselves. I read in The Globe and Mail for September 19 that the Government is now reconsidering cutting environmental jobs after having cut the budget. Now on the eve of the election the Tories want to increase it. The only hope we have is that the Government will bring the budget back to the same level it was in 1984. At least it could do that. When I hear Tories talking about the deficit at this time in our electoral process, I cannot believe my ears. It seems that the Tories are good at rhetoric but they do not live up to promises.
In 1984 the Government promised a net increase of 6 per cent for defence.
A real increase.

A real increase, yes, but when we look at it, not only was there not an increase of 6 per cent in real terms but there was a decrease in the budget in two of the three years for which the Government was responsible. Now the Tories are presenting a White Paper saying the Government will increase the budget by 2 per cent in the coming year. I think Canadians will understand that the Tory Party is good at rhetoric but very thin when it comes to delivering the goods.

Mr. Speaker, that is why I am surprised, in fact there is no word to describe how I feel. I had no intention of rising in this debate, but when again I hear the rhetoric of the Hon. Member who just spoke and who translates the rhetoric and speeches of Conservative Members, I simply do not understand! Perhaps I am naive, or would it be that I am not intelligent enough? What I cannot understand is that on the eve of an election campaign they keep telling us how important the deficit is, yet their Prime Minister is crisscrossing Canada and making promises right, left and centre. As I said earlier, the Toronto Star has put a price tag on all those promises- $14 billion!
How can we have the Prime Minister going around and making promises which will increase the deficit while at the same time his backbenchers stand up in the House and make speeches to show how deeply concerned they are over this issue.
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest these are crocodile tears and that we cannot give credence to these people who in 1984 promised to lower the deficit without raising taxes. Well, they did not accomplish much in terms of deficit reduction, but the taxes certainly went up! So now they are telling us they want to introduce a constitutional amendment outlawing deficits, yet their Prime Minister is travelling across Canada making million-and even billion-dollar promises which will totally
defeat the purpose of the Hon. Member's constitutional amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to participate in this debate this afternoon because it fulfils one of the objectives of private Members' hour, which is to bring before the House certain ideas that are not part of the agenda of a Government or of the opposition Parties but which nonetheless can be introduced into this forum by Members of the House so that we can exchange one with another.
I certainly cannot conceive of anything more pressing in its importance than the subject before us today. The sands of time are obviously running out for this Parliament, but I would hope that if this debate accomplishes nothing more, it will at least put not only on the record but into our minds the importance of addressing the issue of the deficit and the public debt with a sense of priority when the next Parliament resumes.
I think we can take as a satisfaction from this Parliament, which is coming to an end, the progress that has been achieved. We know that when this Parliament assembled, we faced the spectre of a runaway, uncontrollable deficit. We can say at the end of this Parliament that we have achieved control over it. We have arrested the growth of the deficit. Instead of its mounting up from the $38 billion with which we began, it is now $10 billion less. If that rate of progress were to continue, obviously in due course we would get it down to the zero mark, which is the hope of many Hon. Members.
I think we need to address this problem with a greater sense of urgency. We should address it without resorting to the magic wand that some Hon. Members will doubtless want a Government to wave and without berating the Government for not doing this or for doing too much of that. We should face up to the realities that will confront Parliament when it will want to achieve a realistic, practical, achievable elimination of the deficit. Let us look at the possibilities. One of them is to reduce spending.
We have had a measure of fiscal responsibility in this Parliament in so far as the rate of spending before we took office was growing at an annual rate of 14 per cent per year over the preceding four years, and it has been reduced by this Parliament to an average rate of 3.5 per cent, less than the rate of inflation. If we are to make progress in eliminating the deficit, we will have to cut spending still more. Here is where the difficulty arises.
It is all very well for opposition Members to tell the Government that it is making promises that mount up to $12 billion. Which of these commitments would the opposition Members or Members on the Government side of the House want to challenge? One of the recent commitments has been $10 million for a proposed conservation area in Scarborough's


Rouge Valley. Is the Liberal Party against that? Is the NDP against that? Will they criticize the Government for making that commitment?
How about a donation of 123 acres of Downsview Airport land as a site for possibly 5,000 new homes at an estimated value of $60 million? That is $60 million that could come into the public treasury. Certainly money will be spent achieving this development that will provide low-cost housing. Would any Member of any Party oppose that?
Almost every spending proposal that can be put before the House of Commons is one that commends itself to reason because it is filling some human need. It is extremely difficult, therefore, to talk about cutting spending. We face the same difficulty when we move in the other direction, which is to attempt a radical change in the tax system.
I have found over the years that it is usually people right of centre who want to cut spending and people left of centre who want to achieve the no-deficit ideal by changing the tax system, usually by imposing more taxes on someone who is supposed to be paying very little in taxes. The NDP spokesperson is here. I will remind him that years ago, we used to hear a lot about Inco, International Nickel, being the villain. We heard that if only Inco would pay all the tax it should, then we would have no deficit problems at all. We have not heard as much about that lately. I suppose it is because Inco has not been doing very well for several years.
We hear now about certain individuals who are getting away with murder because of the various tax loopholes that are supposed to have been opened. I think we should realize that no matter how we plug those loopholes, and tax reform is certainly heading in the right direction, the mass of taxation will be paid by the mass of people. We have to realize that the mass of people will do the mass of the spending, and they will put up most of the revenue. We have to get away from thinking about Government grants and Government awards and move toward realizing that we are talking about taxpayer grants and taxpayer payments.
The real challenge to us in this debate is to recognize the enormity of the public debt. Every year, we have a deficit we add to the public debt, which has now grown to a size that a few years ago would have seemed beyond comprehension. When we add to that the public debt of the provinces and the municipalities, we begin then to take fright.
While most of the federal debt is owed within Canada, a very large portion of the provincial and municipal debt is owed offshore. Consequently, I believe that one of the challenges that cannot be ignored is the challenge of deficit budgeting and the increase of public debt. We will have to address this, and what I will suggest to address it is a scheduled plan.
It is not possible to eliminate the debt simply by legislation. It is not possible to eliminate it simply by a stroke of the pen. If we were to cut the deficit down to zero in one fell swoop, we would cause such a disruption in the economy that the result
Constitution of Canada
would be worse than the solution. The cure would be worse than the disease. However, it is conceivable, and I put this before the House as a concept to be taken seriously, that we could attempt a schedule of deficit elimination. We could attempt to bring it down by a certain number of percentage points year by year until we reach a balanced budget. That would be done by eliminating certain expenditures and by further tax reform and adjustment, but the real possibility of achieving this is by something which has begun in this Parliament and is due greatly to the economic policies of this Government, and that is by maintaining a buoyant economy.
If we want to eliminate the deficit without removing vital, essential public services, we will have to do it by increasing the revenue possibilities of our economy. We have done a great deal of that in the past four years. The number of people working and thus becoming income tax payers has increased by 1,300,000. We have had a growth of revenue not simply because of increased taxes but primarily because of more taxpayers and because of people earning bigger incomes and thus paying more individually in income tax or in consumer tax and the like. That is the real secret to it, being careful managers of the public purse in the kinds of expenditures that we authorize; being fair, just, and reasonable in a tax system that will eliminate all possibilities of a free ride at the taxpayers' expense and, most of all, carrying out those economic and trade policies which will bring to this country ongoing prosperity and bring to the Government the kind of revenue that makes possible the programs that meet the approval of our people.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to speak on this kind of motion for the umpteenth time in my years here. I have listened to a number of people at various times talking about the deficit and the national debt. What I find most ironic about it is that it was not socialists who rang this up. It was always private enterprise Parties. They have never been to able to explain, or have never even tried to explain, why.
In fact, the socialist Governments of Tommy Douglas, Allan Blakeney, and Woodrow Lloyd, had balanced budgets in a total of 26 of 31 years. I would like to find another political Party of the private enterprise bent somewhere in this country that could claim that kind of a record. So it was not any kind of a socialist ideology that brought about these national debts and deficits.
I am glad that my hon. friend from Lethbridge-Foothills is here to hear my remarks. I read his motion with great interest this morning. One of the myths that he and people like him like to peddle is that governments, like any individual or corporation, have to live within their means. Well, there is one fundamental difference between individuals and corporations on the one hand and Governments on the other. The difference is that the individual or the corporation cannot tax the people


Constitution of Canada
that they owe the money to, but Governments can, Governments do, and Governments will. That sort of mythology which is peddled by some of these outfits and their spokesmen in their places completely overlooks that basic difference between individuals and corporations living within their means and Governments doing so.
I am surprised that my good friend and colleague on the Transport Committee would move a motion like this, unless it is to pacify the Lethbridge Chamber of Commerce, because it is mindless and simplistic. It is a repetition of Reaganomics. It is the Proposition 13 syndrome imported from California.
What I find amusing about this is that the hon. gentleman is challenging his Government. I would be tempted to vote for this stupid motion if it would have the effect that I would like to see. Tie is challenging his Government to bring in a balanced Budget starting tomorrow, which would mean an increase in taxes of at least 50 per cent. It would mean a chopping of at least $10 billion or $15 billion off present expenditures. I could just see the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) jumping up and down with joy about that idea when he is on the verge of calling an election. He might be ignorant but he ain't stupid. However, that is what the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) wants him to be.
I would like to remind my hon. friend that during World War II Canada ran up a national debt and annual deficits that were mind boggling in those days. If fact, if you translated those into 1988 dollars, the national debt and the deficit for every damn year during the war, and the national debt at the end of 1945, was greater than it is now per capita and in total.
I invite my friends to read a book called, I think, The Unnecessary Evil, by Professor Bellam from the University of Manitoba. He throws all these wild eyed, right wing, mindless, simplistic Tory theories about deficits and national debts into a cocked hat.
What happened at the end of the war, Madam Speaker? During the war we turned the entire productive capacity of this nation to work. We had full employment. We did not have enough people to work. I remember working in the shipyards as a 17-year-old and seeing 15-year-old girls catching hot rivets for the war effort. We did it. When the war ended we had this huge national debt and deficit facing us. I will give credit to Mackenzie King, Louis St. Laurent, John Deifenbak-er, and Lester Pearson, who had smarter people around them than present leaders have, except for the NDP.
We had to rebuild most of our industrial infrastructure and capacity. We had to reorder the whole thing from a wartime to a peacetime production. We built up to a half a million homes per year. We are building half that many now and we have waiting lists as long as your arm in every city in this country. But at that time, in the late forties and all during the fifties, we had relatively full employment and we acquired that war debt.
By the way, that debt was wiped out without one nickel of foreign investment. We raised the money ourselves. Yes, our taxes went up. We had to buy war savings certificates and victory bonds through payroll deductions. Everybody did, the nation pitched in. During the late forties and all during the fifties the nation pitched in and we wiped out that debt in something like eight or nine years following World War II, and we had relatively full employment.
If we can do that with a declaration of war, we can do it with a declaration of peace, and we challenge our whole nation to do the kinds of things now that we did then. Madam Speaker, I want to say to my hon. friend, as the gentleman whose book I read said, if you were to reduce unemployment from the present 9 per cent down to 5 or 6 per cent over the next one or two years, you will have wiped out the deficit in three years.
It is not as though nothing needs to be done. We can put a quarter million people to work cleaning up our air and water. That will require billions of dollars that we will have to borrow. All those people are put to work, they pay taxes and that pays for the borrowing. I am an innocent stubble jumping prairie boy, but that has always worked before. It seems to make sense.
I talked about the requirement for places for people to live. Every city in this country has a list as long as one's arm for chronic care beds, hospital beds, low income housing and public housing. That would require the construction industry to go to work like it did during wartime. We could cut the national debt in half if those guys over there had something more than the imagination of a doorknob and did not rely on the theories of the 17th and 18th centuries, let alone the 19th century. It is outmoded thinking. It does not work. It never has and never will. It only appeals to the mindless selfish greed of those who ask: "What is in it for me and to hell with everybody else". Again, that is imported from south of the 49th parallel.
Canada is something more and better than that. I do not want to hear any more silly motions. What if there was a national emergency, a natural disaster which required the federal Government to spend $10 billion?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Read the motion.

What would happen to the balanced budget? I expected more from the Hon. Member for Lethbridge- Foothills than what I see in this motion. This motion should get the contempt it deserves. Perhaps we should pass it to see what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has to say about it.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words on the motion brought forward by my friend, the Hon. Member for Lethbridge- Foothills (Mr. Thacker). The motion states:


That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the
advisability of amending the Constitution of Canada so as to require the
government to submit a balanced budget except:-
Of course, the Elon. Member for Regina West (Mr, Benjamin) did not bother reading "except", which states:
(a)	in times of a declared national emergency or disaster, or
(b)	if the deficit receives parliamentary approval by a two-thirds majority.
I have great respect for the Elon. Member for Lethbridge- Foothills. I have served in the House with him since 1984, and have learned to listen to him carefully. I certainly have a great deal of respect for the things he says, the ideas he puts forward, and the actions and initiatives he takes.
The motion which he has put forward today is one in which I can share in a sympathetic way many of his feelings. We have an enormous deficit today and have had for a number of years. The Hon. Member's point of view is one that is shared not only by Members on the Government side of the House but by many Canadians.
I was knocking on doors yesterday and a number of people confronted me on the deficit issue. They were very concerned about the deficit situation and the actions the Government had or had not taken with respect to it during the last four years.
As one who served in municipal government for many years, like the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar), I am certainly most sympathetic with the concept put forward because municipal governments must balance their budgets by law. They are required not to spend any more money than they raise for current expenditures. This is a concept which certainly raises a lot of sympathy in my soul.
However, I must depart from the position taken by my hon. friend, the Member for Lethbridge-Foothills. During the last two centuries, until the Great Depression of the 1930's, it was traditional economic thinking, traditional government thinking and traditional business thinking that we should have balanced budgets and no Government should spend more than it takes in. It was traditional thinking that we should always make sure that we either raise enough money to pay or cut our cloth according to the money we raise so that there will be a balanced budget.
That concept had some problems in the 1930's, with the Great Depression. The enormous economic difficulties we suffered at that time caused people to begin re-examining that issue and determine whether or not it made sense in all circumstances to have a balanced budget. The Hon. Member for Regina West has raised this in a practical sense, but in a theoretic sense, prior to the 1930's an economist named John Maynard Keynes wrote a book entitled "The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money". He really turned the world of economics and the world of government financing upside down.
That book and the propositions that were put forward by John Maynard Keynes, later Lord Keynes, advocated what has become known as counter cyclical fiscal policy on the part of
Constitution of Canada
government. According to that policy, when a country is faced with hard economic times, it should be offset with expenditures to try to raise the level of demand in the country in order to encourage people to start businesses, to spend money and to put people back to work.
It may not be as well known that Lord Keynes had another part to his theory. It was not just to spend money and have deficit financing if there were hard times. He advocated that one in fact run a surplus, perhaps not enormous, but a surplus in good times. When people were working and the economy was booming and there were inflationary pressures, he suggested that we should not be running a deficit but should be running a surplus and trying to tax away some of that excess of spending power in order to keep inflation under control at the same time as running full employment.
The Keynes theory as set out in his book of general theory, employment, interest and money back in the 1920's was an anti-cylical policy. It was to run a deficit in bad times and run a surplus in good times. He advocated that policy very strongly through the 1930s and the times of depression. Some politicians and government leaders listened to his proposals, but even the ones who listened had some difficulty because it was certainly revolutionary in the sense of the then accepted economic theory. People said that this was really extreme leftism, communism, and would destroy capitalism. In fact, the theories of John Maynard Keynes, when put into practice, actually supported the capitalist process and made sure it worked.
Some people tried to put his theories into effect. Here in North America, Franklin Delano Roosevelt made some effort to put that into effect. In Canada, R. B. Bennett, the Prime Minister of Canada in the middle 1930s, made some effort to put it into effect. They did not go quite far enough to make it work. As my friend from Regina has pointed out, it took the Second World War to really force us into expenditures of the size that were necessary to bring us out of that enormous depression of the 1930s, to right the situation again. It was because of those expenditures and, quite frankly, the deficits that were run at that time that we did come out of the Great Depression of the 1930s.
It was during the closing years of the Second World War when people finally began to realize what Lord Keynes had put before them. They saw a method of maintaining full employment, keeping inflation at a reasonable rate, merely by fiscal policy, not by running up the Bank of Canada rate to enormous rates like they did a few years ago in the 1980s, but by controlling inflation with fiscal policy, not monetary policy, and taxing away those inflationary pressures.
Immediately after the Second World War, that is the sort of policy that the federal Government in Canada put into effect. I have to give an enormous amount of credit-I am not sure if the Prime Minister of the day deserves that credit, but his


Constitution of Canada
Finance Ministers certainly do; Mr. Ilsley and Mr. Abbott. Mr. Abbott passed away a short time ago. I am a great admirer of those two gentlemen because I think they truly put into effect the other side of Keynes' policies, the side where you actually ran surpluses in good times. But the problem was that that was not politically acceptable. Unfortunately, it is not very nice for politicians to go out and tell the public that they are going to raise taxes to run on a surplus. The public, understandably, does not want to pay higher taxes and, as a result, that sort of a policy became very unpopular. I am one who thinks that it was one of the main reasons why, in 1957, the Government of Prime Minister St. Laurent lost the election to Prime Minister Diefenbaker. The Government of the day, in good times, was running a surplus and keeping taxes at a rate to actually run a surplus on its current account.
You know where we have gone from there. The Government decided that since that was not politically popular, from then on it was going to make sure that it ran the country in a politically popular way. Finance Minister after Finance Minister has been afraid to raise taxes and to run that surplus in good times. As a result of that we have worked ourselves deeper and deeper into the debt that we have. It is only in the last four years that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has tried to address it. He has not tried to address it all at once, but has tried to address the problem slowly but surely.
With the greatest of respect to my hon. friend from Lethbridge-and I know my time has come to an end-I would like to say that while I have great sympathy for his proposition, I think if we practised a little Keynesian economics in this country and if Governments had the intestinal fortitude to do that, we would not have any problems with deficits or inflation or full employment. We would have the kind of economy that we all want in Canada; full employment with reasonable crisis under control at all times.

Madam
Speaker, I rise to speak to this because I certainly agree with a lot that the previous speaker has said. I am glad to see that some members of the Conservative caucus are taking on some of our program of full employment and responsible fiscal management, because they certainly have not done that in the last four years.
I see the Government going out and buying its way through every vote, taking a populace kind of approach to policy rather than looking at some good-management, long-term planning.
I recommend that Members look at the management of the Government of A1 Blakeney in Saskatchewan. He had three surplus Budgets in the last three Budgets and he was not afraid to say to the people of Saskatchewan that this is how we are managing. It has been downhill ever since the Conservatives took over in that province. That gives you a sense of what fiscal management is all about.
However, my approach to this would be a little different than what we have heard today. I have great concerns about
using our Constitution to contravene the political will of the country. If we want to build a strengthened democracy in this country, we have to put forward political platforms, let the people know how we feel about them, and let the people vote one way or another.
We have to be very careful about how we are using our Constitution. It is a simplistic approach to suggest that we can just make a constitutional amendment on things and then let the courts look after it. As responsible human beings who are democratically elected, it is up to us to put in place the kind of policies that we think are responsible and accountable. Bringing forward something like this to amend the Constitution is a lack of faith and trust in the democratic process and in the people who electus. I have great respect for those people.
I do not always agree with them, but I have great respect for those who elect us. I think that they have the right to forge the avenue that we are to take.
After the next election I think that many members of the Conservative caucus are going to see that they did not forge that road when they had such a huge majority. They could have had their full employment and a real tax reform. They could have been able to say to the people of Canada that they do not have to have just a small group of rich people getting richer.
If we look at the tax system, we recognize that there is about S29 billion in tax expenditures. Loopholes could be closed. With one stroke, it almost starts to look at dealing with the carrying of that deficit that is about $32 billion.
Those are the kinds of things that you have to look at and say to the Canadian people that it is not as simple as raising taxes or not raising taxes and this kind of thing. It is looking at good management and accountable fiscal policies that give you some long-term planning where you cannot be responsible.
Sometimes people have suggested that municipalities legislatively cannot accumulate debt. That, too, is a bit of smoke and mirrors. Municipalities have the ability of launching debentures. Some of those debentures can be very much an encumbrance on their assets.
In municipal government we adopted a policy that was called "pay as you go". Instead of increasing the debenture, we paid for the things in the good times so that we would have the infrastructure there and they would not fall apart. Proposition 13 did the opposite. It was a legislative proposition. The infrastructures in the cities of California fell apart. The kind of terrible disparities that came into that municipal legislation was really tragic. It showed that you cannot approach government in the simplistic way. I think it is six o'clock.
